title: Zones and junk defenses
text:
Guarding areas instead of players, and hybrids built to erase one scorer.
All families · 7 terms · 0 full, 0 partial, 7 short

1-3-1 zone
One at the top, three across the free-throw line, one on the baseline; built to trap and force long passes.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense


2-3 zone
Two defenders up top and three across the baseline, packing the paint.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense, 3-2 zone


3-2 zone
Three across the free-throw line extended and two on the blocks, pressuring shooters at the cost of the glass.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense


Box-and-one
Four defenders in a box zone with one chasing the opponent’s best player man-to-man.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense, Junk defense


Junk defense
Also: combination defense
Any zone-and-man hybrid built to take one player out of a game.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Box-and-one


Match-up zone
A zone whose defenders take the player in their area man-to-man while he is there.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also Zone defense, Man-to-man


Zone defense
Each defender guards an area rather than a player.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.6 · See also 2-3 zone, Match-up zone, Man-to-man

title: Transition defense
text:
Rim, ball, then match up. In that order.
All families · 13 terms · 11 full, 2 partial, 0 short

Crash or get back
The trade-off, decided per team and per shot, between sending players to the offensive glass and sending them back on defense.
Why it is run. Offensive rebounds are worth a lot; giving up run-outs costs a lot. There is no free answer; a team picks a rule and the rule depends on who is on the floor.
offense / defense · Transition · partial · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Floor balance, Leak out


Cross-match
A deliberate transition match-up that is not the half-court assignment, such as a wing taking the opposing big so the big can run to the rim.
Why it is run. The defensive big is often the last man back. Letting the nearest wing take the offensive big, and the big take the wing, keeps the rim protected.
What beats it. The offense attacking the size mismatch before the defense can swap back.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Match up, Scram switch


Floor balance
Also: safety, get-back man
The offensive team’s rule for who stays back on a shot so the other team cannot run.
Why it is run. Every offensive rebounder is one fewer player getting back. Most teams designate one or two players who retreat as the shot goes up.
What beats it. The offense crashing everyone and betting the extra possessions outweigh the run-outs.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Crash or get back, Leak out


Jam the rebounder
Also: pressure the outlet
Pressuring the defensive rebounder as he lands, and denying the outlet man, so the break starts late.
Why it is run. A break that starts one second late is a break that meets a set defense. The player nearest the rebounder stays on him instead of turning to run.
What beats it. A rebounder who outlets on the way down, and a second outlet option.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Outlet pass, Stop the ball


Load to the ball
Retreating defenders shading toward the side the ball is on, so the ball-handler sees bodies and the far side is left for last.
Why it is run. The ball scores; the far-side player has to be passed to first. Loading to the ball takes away the drive and dares the long skip pass.
What beats it. The skip pass to the weak-side corner.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Stop the ball


Match up
Also: find a body, find your man
The last job getting back: each defender taking a player, not necessarily his own, so every attacker is guarded.
Why it is run. In transition there is no time to find your assignment. The rule is to take the nearest unguarded attacker and sort out the mismatches after the possession is under control.
What beats it. The offense hunting the mismatch that the emergency match-up created.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Transition defense, Cross-match, Scram switch


No layups
Also: make them shoot over you
The transition rule that the paint is protected before anything else, so the shot conceded is a jumper, never a layup.
Why it is run. A rule a tired player can follow. When a defender does not know where to go, he goes to the paint.
What beats it. The transition three.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Transition three


Pick-up point
How far up the floor the defense meets the ball; at the free-throw line extended, at half court, or full court.
Why it is run. A higher pick-up slows the offense earlier but costs the defender ground behind him. Teams pick it by their personnel and by how much they trust their rim protection.
defense · Transition · partial · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Stop the ball, Press


Protect the rim first
Also: build the wall, paint first
The first job getting back: the first defenders sprint to the paint, not to a man, and then close out from there.
Why it is run. A layup is the shot transition gives up most and costs most. Sprinting to the paint takes it away; everything else is closed out to from the inside.
What beats it. The corner fill and the transition three, which are the shots the offense takes when the paint is closed.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Transition defense, Stop the ball, Corner fill


Stop the ball
Also: pick up the ball, pick-up point
One defender meeting the ball-handler early to slow the dribble and turn the break into a half-court possession.
Why it is run. A ball-handler at full speed beats a defender back-pedalling. Met early, he has to slow down, and the defense behind him gets the seconds it needs.
What beats it. The hit-ahead pass, which moves the ball past the pick-up point without dribbling into it.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Pick-up point, Hit-ahead pass


Tandem defense
Also: I formation, two-on-one defense
Two defenders against three attackers lined up one in front of the other: the front man takes the ball, the back man takes the first pass, then they rotate.
Why it is run. Side by side, two defenders leave the middle open. In a line, the ball is met at the free-throw line and the rim is still protected; the first pass is taken by the back man and the front man drops to the rim.
What beats it. Swinging the ball twice fast, or a shooter stopping for the three instead of running to the rim.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Numbers advantage, Protect the rim first


Transition defense
Also: getting back
Everything the defense does between losing the ball and being set in the half court.
Why it is run. The offense is trying to score before the defense is organized. The defense’s job, in order, is to protect the rim, stop the ball, and then match up.
What beats it. The push and the hit-ahead, which try to beat the defense to those three jobs.
defense · Transition · full · Taught in lecture 4.1 · See also Protect the rim first, Stop the ball, Match up, Floor balance


Transition take foul
Also: take foul, Euro foul
A deliberate foul on the ball early in a break to stop the play before the numbers advantage can be used.
Why it is run. Trading two free throws for a near-certain layup was, for years, worth it. It is worth less than it was.
What beats it. None on the floor; the counter came from the rule book.
What changed. From the 2022-23 season the NBA penalizes a transition take foul with one free throw, shot by any player on the offended team, plus possession, so the foul no longer trades the break for two free throws.

Source: registry nba-2022-take-foul. NBA.com, dated July 13, 2022. Verbatim: “Beginning with the 2022-23 NBA season”, then two bullets: “The offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “The offensive team will retain possession of the ball.” A first URL remembered for this entry returned 404 and was replaced; the entry was not published on the remembered one. title: Sets and systems
text:
Alignments, called plays, and the rule-based offenses that run without a call.
All families · 14 terms · 12 full, 1 partial, 1 short

4-on-3
The advantage behind a trap: four attackers against the three defenders who did not trap.
Why it is run. Two defenders on the ball leaves three to guard four; the weak-side low man cannot cover the dunker spot and the corner at once, and the pass out of the trap goes to whichever he leaves.
What beats it. Rotations quick enough to cover four spots with three men until the trap recovers, and a trap timed so the shot clock does the rest.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.3 · See also Blitz, Short roll


Delay
Also: 5-out delay
An early-offense alignment with the big at the top holding the ball and the four others spaced, from which he hands off, screens or reverses.
Why it is run. With the big holding the ball at the arc and nobody in the paint, his defender must choose between guarding him twenty-five feet out and protecting a rim nobody is near; either choice opens the handoff or the drive.
What beats it. The big’s defender guarding him at the arc and denying the handoff, or the defense switching every handoff so no cutter gets the ball moving.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also 5-out, Dribble handoff, Zoom


Dribble drive motion
Also: DDM, dribble drive
A spread offense with no post player in the lane, built on driving gaps and kicking out or dropping off when the help comes.
Why it is run. With the lane empty and the big in the weak-side dunker spot, a drive into a double gap forces one help defender to choose between the rim and the corner, and the pass goes to whoever he left.
What beats it. Guarding the drive with one man and never helping, which needs defenders who stay in front, or walling off the middle and conceding the pull-up.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.9 · See also 5-out, Drive, Kick-out, Gap


Flex offense
Also: flex cut
A continuity offense whose repeating unit is a baseline cross screen followed by a down screen for the screener.
Why it is run. A cross screen and a down screen for the screener return the floor to its own starting shape, so the sequence can run again until one defender is late.
What beats it. Switching both screens, which is available to a team of similar-sized players, or going under the cross screen every time and living with the seal.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.9 · See also Cross screen, Pin-down, Ram


Flow offense
Offense that runs continuously from transition into half-court actions without a called play, governed by rules for who screens and who spaces.
offense · Early offense · short · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Early offense, Motion offense


Horns
An alignment with two bigs at the elbows, two shooters in the corners and the ball at the top.
Why it is run. Two bigs at the elbows and two shooters in the corners empties the paint, puts two screeners one pass from the ball, and makes several different plays look identical for the first two seconds.
What beats it. Switching everything, which removes the screens and concedes the mismatches, or a big at the level of the ball screen with the low man tagging the roller.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.8 · See also Elbow, Pick-and-roll


Isolation
Also: iso
Clearing a side so one player can attack one defender.
Why it is run. When one attacker beats one defender by himself, the best use of the other four is to stand where their defenders cannot help.
What beats it. A defender who stays in front; or sending a second defender early and living with the pass out.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Mismatch, Switch


Mismatch
A matchup the offense can exploit, such as a big guarding a guard on the perimeter or a guard guarding a big in the post.
Why it is run. A switch leaves a big on a guard or a guard on a big, and both halves are attackable: the guard drives the slower man, the big posts the smaller one.
What beats it. The scram switch, switching back at the first dead ball, or a roster similar enough in size that no switch creates one.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Switch, Isolation, Early seal


Motion offense
Offense run from rules rather than a script, where players read the defense and cut or screen accordingly.
Why it is run. Rules attached to the pass produce screening and cutting continuously, so the defense must guard correctly every time, and the offense needs no call and can be run at any tempo.
What beats it. Switching everything, which turns every screen into a non-event and dares the offense to win one-on-one; or physical denial of the first pass.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Flow offense, Set play, Read and react


Pistol
Also: 21, Nash action
An early-offense entry where the guard passes ahead to the wing and follows the pass into a handoff or a quick ball screen.
Why it is run. Passing ahead and following the pass turns the best ball-handler’s defender’s one relaxed step into a handoff taken at speed toward the middle, with a big’s screen already coming.
What beats it. Switching the handoff, or top-locking the guard so he cannot follow his pass.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Dribble handoff, Early offense


Princeton offense
A read-based offense built on a high-post entry, back cuts against overplay, and screens away from the ball.
Why it is run. The high post passes and every denial becomes a back cut, so a defense that presses the perimeter gives up layups and a defense that sags gives up the catch.
What beats it. Refusing to deny: play a step off, concede the perimeter catch and take away the cuts, so the offense has to shoot over a set defense.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.9 · See also Back cut, Motion offense, Read and react


Read and react
A conceptual offense where every off-ball player has a rule for each thing the ball does.
Why it is run. Every player has a reaction to the drive, executed before the drive resolves, so the three outlets are already moving when the help commits.
What beats it. A defense that never helps, so no reaction is triggered; or shrinking the floor so every drive is into a single gap.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.11 · See also Motion offense, 45 cut, Lift


Set play
A scripted sequence run to get a particular shot for a particular player.
Why it is run. Five players know what is coming and the defense does not; the cost is three or four seconds of setup during which the defense gets organized, which is why teams run them after timeouts, for a specific player, and at the end of a period.
offense · Half court · partial · Taught in lecture 3.8 · See also Motion offense, ATO


Zipper
A player cutting from the block straight up the lane line off a down screen to catch at the top.
Why it is run. A cut straight up the lane line off a screen delivers the catch at the slot with the whole floor in front of the catcher, and usually straight into a ball screen from the man who just screened.
What beats it. Top-locking the cutter so he cannot come up the lane line, conceding the back cut, or switching the screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.8 · See also Pin-down

title: Pick-and-roll coverages
text:
How two defenders handle a ball screen. This decides a team’s defensive identity.
All families · 9 terms · 0 full, 0 partial, 9 short

At the level
The big meets the handler at the level of the screen, between drop and hedge.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage, Hedge


Blitz
Also: trap
Both defenders trap the handler at the screen, leaving three defenders against four.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Short roll, 4-on-3, Hedge


Drop coverage
Also: drop
Against a ball screen the big stays back near the paint while the guard fights over the screen.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Pick-and-roll, Snake dribble, Ice


Hedge
Also: show, hard hedge
The big jumps out above the screen to stop the handler, then recovers to the roller.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage, Blitz


Ice
Also: blue, down, push
On a side ball screen the on-ball defender forces the handler toward the sideline and away from the screen, with the big dropped toward the baseline.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage, Step-up screen


Man-to-man
Each defender is responsible for one attacker wherever he goes.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Zone defense, Switch


Next
Also: next switch, up-to-touch
A switch called by the big on a ball screen where the guard’s defender stays attached until the big has the handler.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.5 · See also Switch


Switch
The two defenders in a screen trade assignments.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.5 · See also Scram switch, Mismatch, Peel switch


Under
Also: go under
The on-ball defender goes beneath the screen, conceding the pull-up to keep the drive in front.
defense · Half court · short · Taught in lecture 4.3 · See also Drop coverage

title: Off-ball screens
text:
Screens for players without the ball, which is how shooters get open.
All families · 11 terms · 11 full, 0 partial, 0 short

Back screen
A screen set behind a defender, out of his view, so the cutter can go to the rim.
Why it is run. A defender watching the ball cannot see a screen set on his back, so the man he guards is at the rim before he can follow.
What beats it. Feeling the screen and going under it toward the rim early, conceding the pop, or switching every back screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Flare screen, Rip screen, Spain pick-and-roll


Cross screen
A screen set across the lane so a big can cut from one block to the other for a post catch.
Why it is run. A screen across the lane, block to block, gets a big a post catch with his defender sealed on his back, because the defender must choose between going over the screen and going under it into the passing lane.
What beats it. The defender going over the top to reach the block first and fronting the post, or a low man who bumps the cutter in the lane.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Post-up, Block


Elevator screen
Also: elevator doors
A shooter runs between two screeners who then step together to close the gap on his defender.
Why it is run. Two screeners who close the gap the moment the shooter is through stop his defender dead with two bodies at once, and it is the one screen set after the cutter has passed.
What beats it. Going round the outside of one screener before the doors close, conceding a step on the catch, or switching one screener’s defender onto the shooter as he comes through.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Stagger


Flare screen
A screen that lets a perimeter player fade away from the ball along the arc, punishing a defender who cheats toward the ball.
Why it is run. A defender who cheats toward the ball can be screened on the side facing away from it, so his man fades along the arc for a skip pass the defense was leaning away from.
What beats it. A defender who stays on the line between his man and the ball and never cheats, or a switch.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Pin-down, Back screen


Floppy
A shooter under the rim chooses either side, one with a single screen and one with a stagger.
Why it is run. A shooter under the rim with a single screen one way and a stagger the other reads his defender’s first step and goes the other way; the defender cannot be right about both sides.
What beats it. Going under everything and meeting him at the wing, conceding the curl, or switching every screen so a fresh defender waits on either side.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Stagger, Pin-down


Hammer
A baseline drive on one side with a back screen on the other, freeing a shooter into the weak-side corner for a drift pass.
Why it is run. The weak-side helper who sinks on a baseline drive is doing what he was taught, and the back screen punishes him for it; the shooter drifts to the corner and the pass comes along the baseline under the rim.
What beats it. Helping with the eyes and not the feet, so the shooter is never left, or the X-out rotation in which the big’s defender takes the corner and the wing defender takes the big.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Back screen, Corner


Loop
A cutter running a triple stagger along the baseline from one wing to the other.
Why it is run. Three screens along a path the defender must run in full, with the catch waiting at the far wing.
What beats it. Cutting across the lane under the screens to meet the cutter at the far wing, conceding the curl on the first screen, or a switch at any of the three.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Stagger


Pin-down
Also: down screen
A screen set facing the baseline so a player near the rim can cut up to the perimeter for a catch.
Why it is run. A screen facing the baseline lets a shooter who started near the rim arrive at the perimeter with his defender behind the screen, and gives him four reads off it (curl, fade, straight, back cut) that the defender’s choice decides.
What beats it. Top-locking the shooter so he cannot reach the screen, conceding the back cut to take away the shot, or switching the screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Flare screen, Stagger, Top-lock


Rip screen
A back screen across the lane, usually for a player who has just set a screen himself.
Why it is run. A defender who has just helped on a screen is standing exactly where a back screen wants him, so the screener he left rips to the rim behind him.
What beats it. The screener’s defender never leaving him to help, or a switch.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Back screen


Stagger
Also: staggered screens
Two off-ball screens in a row in the same direction for one cutter.
Why it is run. Two screens in the same direction make the defender right twice; the wrong side of the first is the wrong side of the second, and the second screener can slip if his own defender jumps out.
What beats it. Going under both screens and meeting the shooter at the catch, conceding the curl, or switching the second screen.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.5 · See also Pin-down, Floppy


Wedge
A player receives an off-ball screen to the top and immediately turns to set a ball screen.
Why it is run. A side screen for the big before he screens the ball makes his defender late to the pick-and-roll, the same idea as the ram from a different direction.
What beats it. Switching the first screen so the nearest defender guards the ball screen, or the big’s defender going under the first screen and beating him to the top.
offense · Half court · full · Taught in lecture 3.6 · See also Pick-and-roll, Ram

title: Early offense
text:
The first action after the break, against a defense that is back but not organized.
All families · 2 terms · 2 full, 0 partial, 0 short

Early offense
Actions run in the first seconds of a half-court possession, against a defense that is back but not yet organized.
Why it is run. A defense that got back has still not matched up, and its big is often trailing. Early offense hits that seam with one quick action before the defense settles.
What beats it. Matching up while sprinting back, and having the big sprint rather than jog.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Drag screen, Pistol, Delay, Secondary break


Trailer flip
The trailing big arriving at the top to take a reversal pass and swing the ball to the other side.
Why it is run. The trailing big is the one attacker the defense has not matched; taking the reversal at the top and swinging it in one motion gets the ball to the weak side before the defense has shifted.
What beats it. The big’s defender sprinting to the top with him so the reversal is contested, or the weak-side defenders shifting on the flight of the first pass.
offense · Early offense · full · Taught in lecture 3.2 · See also Trailer, Delay

title: The floor and spacing
text:
Where things are, and why five players standing in the right places is most of offense.
All families · 16 terms · 0 full, 1 partial, 15 short

4-out 1-in
An alignment with four players outside the arc and one inside, usually in the dunker spot or on a block.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also 5-out, Dunker spot


5-out
An alignment with all five players outside the arc and the paint empty.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also 4-out 1-in, Spacing, Delay


Block
The painted mark on the lane line near the rim; the traditional low-post spot.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Post-up, Dunker spot

The spot where the three-point line meets the sideline; the closest three to the rim, and the spot the low man has to leave to help.

Dunker spot
Also: short corner
The baseline spot just outside the lane, below the block, where a non-shooting big waits for lobs, dump-offs and offensive rebounds.
offense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Block, Lob


Elbow
Where the free-throw line meets the lane line; a hub for handoffs and high-post play.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Pinch post, Horns


Gap
Also: double gap, single gap
The space between two perimeter players; a single gap is one spot wide, a double gap is two, and a driver wants the double.

offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also Help side, Dig, Stunt

The half-circle in front of the rim inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 4.4 · See also The paint, Verticality

The perimeter spot above the arc roughly in line with the lane line, between the top and the wing.
offense / defense · General · short · Taught in lecture 3.10 · See also Wing, Top of the key, Corner

Keeping players far enough apart that one defender cannot guard two of them.
Why it is run. Standing so that no defender can guard two attackers at once is what makes every drive, cut and screen in this chapter work; the measurement is the gap, and a double gap is the one worth attacking.

title: Offense
text:
The offense’s job in one sentence: get two defenders to guard one player, then pass to the one nobody is guarding. Every phase below is a different way to force that.


Offense lectures in reading order.


Lecture
What it teaches




2.2 The Analytics That Drove It
Points per possession as the currency, the arithmetic of the corner three, gravity, and how much of the modern game follows from one division.


3.1 Transition Offense
The break in the order it unfolds: the outlet and push, the lanes and rim run, the numbers read, the trailer and secondary break, how transition is counted.


3.2 Early Offense
The first action against a defense that is back but not organized: the drag and double drag, pistol, delay and the handoff, zoom, get action, and the flow that joins them.


3.3 On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family
The screen, the pick-and-roll, roll, pop, short roll, the step-up screen, the snake dribble, the lob and the 4-on-3 behind a trap.


3.4 On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions
Ram, Spain, ghost, slip and twist: the ball-screen actions that exist because the coverages got good at guarding the plain pick-and-roll, and the names heard for them that are not yet entries.


3.5 Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
Pin-down, flare, back screen, rip, cross screen, stagger: the six shapes a screen away from the ball can take, and the four reads a cutter makes off any of them.


3.6 Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
Elevator, Hammer, Floppy, Loop and Wedge: the named actions built from the six screen shapes, each taken apart into its parts, plus the names heard that have no entry yet.


3.7 Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
What a player without the ball does when nobody screens for him: the post-up and the early seal, the cuts that punish a defender’s eyes (45, back, flash, stampede), the cuts that use a body (UCLA, Iverson), give and go, high-low, and the lift and pinch post that keep the floor spaced.


3.8 Sets and Systems
The alignment a team starts from and the script it runs: Horns, Zipper, the set play as a concept, and the named sets and plays heard that have no entry yet.


3.9 Continuity and Read-Based Systems
Offenses that do not end: Princeton, Flex and dribble drive motion, each a whole system rather than an action, and what distinguishes a continuity from a set play.


3.10 Spacing and Roles
The floor and its spots, the alignments, the gap and why its width decides everything, the drive, kick-out and skip pass, and the five roles as they are actually played now.


3.11 Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
Offense run from rules rather than a script: motion, read and react, isolation and the mismatch, and the synthesis of every beaten-by slot in this chapter.


3.12 Special Situations, Offense
Possessions that do not start with a live ball or a set defense: BLOB and SLOB, the box and stack sets they run from, the ATO, the press break and zone offense.


3.13 Late Clock, Offense
When the clock, not the defense, is the constraint: the late-clock possession and the 2-for-1.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
New terms introduced (13): Crash or get back, Cross-match, Floor balance, Jam the rebounder, Load to the ball, Match up, No layups, Pick-up point, Protect the rim first, Stop the ball, Tandem defense, Transition defense, Transition take foul. Diagrams: 2.
Lecture 3.1 ended by calling every transition advantage a deadline: the numbers last until the defense is back, the empty rim lasts until the big is home, the unguarded trailer lasts until his man arrives. Transition defense is the work of bringing those deadlines forward, and it is unusual among defensive subjects in having almost no scheme to it. There is no coverage to choose. There are three jobs, they come in a fixed order, and the order is the whole lesson.
The order is rim, ball, match up. First the paint is protected, so the shot the offense cannot get is the layup. Then the ball is stopped, so the break slows to a walk. Only then does each defender find a man. Every transition breakdown a coach shows on film is one of these done out of order: a defender who ran to his man while the rim was empty, or a defender who found a body while nobody had the ball.
This lecture takes the three jobs in that order. Section 1 is the rim, Section 2 is the ball, Section 3 is the outnumbered case where both have to be done by two players, and Section 4 is matching up. Section 5 goes back before the shot, to the decisions a defense makes while it is still on offense. Section 6 is the take foul, and what the rule book did to it. Each coverage is set out in a card with four slots, and each card’s last slot names the action from lecture 3.1 that is built to beat it.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
1 Protect the rim first
The first defenders back do not run to a man. They run to the paint. This is the rule behind protect the rim first, and it exists because of how the shots the offense might take rank. A layup is the shot transition produces most and the shot it produces most efficiently, and a defender who runs to a wing while the paint is empty has taken away a corner three and conceded a dunk. Sprinting to the paint takes the layup away, and every other shot is then closed out to from the inside (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Protect the rim first. Three retreating defenders each sprint to the paint before turning to a shooter. The layup is taken away first; the corners are closed out to second, from the inside. This is what the offense’s wide lanes are trying to prevent.



The phrase a coach uses for this is no layups, and it is a rule chosen for a tired player. A defender sprinting back at full speed cannot process where five attackers are. He can process one instruction, and the instruction is: paint. When he gets there he looks up, and only then does he pick a shooter to close out to. The order costs a beat on the perimeter and buys the rim, and the rim is worth more.
Two refinements follow. The first is that defenders load to the ball as they retreat: they shade toward the side the ball is on, so the ball-handler sees bodies in front of him and the far side of the floor is the last thing the defense worries about. The ball scores; the far corner has to be passed to first, and a long cross-court pass is the pass a retreating defense can most afford to allow. The second is that the first big back goes to the rim regardless of who he is guarding. If the opposing big has beaten him down the floor, that is a problem for the match-up in Section 4, not a reason to leave the paint.






Assignment


The first two defenders back sprint to the paint, below the ball, and stop the layup. They close out to shooters only after the paint is protected.


Concedes


The first open three, usually to a wing who stopped at the arc. This is a deliberate trade.


Requires


Effort and one rule. No reading is needed, which is the point.


Beaten by


Running the lanes with a corner fill, which puts shooters exactly where the paint-first defender has to leave them, and the transition three that follows.





Coverage 1: Protect the rim first: the one rule a sprinting player can follow.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
2 Stop the ball
A ball-handler at full speed is a problem for the whole defense, because every defender behind him is back-pedalling and every decision they make is made a second late. Stopping the ball is one defender meeting the ball-handler early enough that he has to slow down, and the value is not in the stop itself but in the seconds it gives the four players behind.
Where the ball is met is the pick-up point, and it is a choice. A defense that picks the ball up at the free-throw line extended in the back court slows the break earlier but leaves that defender further from the paint if he is beaten. A defense that picks it up at the top of the key in the front court gives up the early dribble but keeps its shape. The choice is made by personnel: a team with a rim protector it trusts picks up higher, because a beaten defender is not the end of the possession. A team without one picks up lower and keeps its bodies in the paint.
The defender who takes the ball says so. The one word of communication that transition defense cannot do without is the one that tells the other four that the ball is handled, because the second job is done only once and a defense with two players on the ball has three on the other four.






Assignment


One defender, usually the nearest guard, meets the ball-handler at the pick-up point and turns him, calling it so nobody else comes.


Concedes


The pass. The ball-handler who is stopped will look to move the ball, and the defense is betting that the receivers are covered by Section 1.


Requires


A defender who can slow a guard at speed without fouling, and a pick-up point the whole team agrees on.


Beaten by


The hit-ahead pass, which moves the ball past the pick-up point before the pick-up defender has arrived, and the push by pass rather than by dribble.





Coverage 2: Stop the ball: the second job, done once, called out loud.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
3 Outnumbered
When two defenders face three attackers, or one faces two, the two jobs above have to be done by the same players, and there is a shape for that. It is tandem defense, and the shape is a line, not a row (Figure 2).






Figure 2: Tandem. Two defenders in a line down the middle. The front man steps up to the ball at the free-throw line; when the ball is passed to a wing, the back man takes the receiver and the front man drops to the rim. The middle is never open.



Two defenders side by side leave the middle open, and the ball-handler from lecture 3.1 goes straight down it. Two defenders in a line, one at the free-throw line and one near the rim, present the ball-handler with a defender in front of him and a defender behind that one. The front man stops the ball. When the ball is passed to a wing, the back man goes to the receiver, and the front man drops to the rim to take the back man’s place. Then, if the ball is passed again, they rotate again. The wing pass is conceded; the layup is not, and neither is the drive down the middle.
The tandem holds until help arrives, and it is a delaying action rather than a solution. What it prevents is the outcome the numbers break is designed for: a defender who steps to the ball with nobody behind him.






Assignment


The two defenders form a line in the middle. Front takes the ball; back takes the first pass; front drops to the rim; repeat until the third defender arrives.


Concedes


A wing jumper, and the second pass if it is fast enough.


Requires


Two defenders who know which of them is front, decided by who arrives first and never argued about.


Beaten by


The numbers advantage used patiently: the ball stays in the middle, the wings stay wide, and the ball swings twice faster than the tandem can rotate.





Coverage 3: Tandem: a line, not a row, and the middle is never open.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
4 Match up
Once the rim is protected and the ball is stopped, the break is over and the defense has a possession to defend. It still has no assignments. The third job is matching up, and the rule for it is the one a tired player can follow: take the nearest unguarded attacker, whoever he is, and say his number. A defender who runs past an open attacker to find his own man has left a shooter open for the time it takes to get there, and in transition that time is a shot.
The consequence is that transition match-ups are often wrong by design. A wing ends up on a big; a big ends up on a guard. This is a cross-match, and it is sometimes deliberate: when the offensive big has beaten the defensive big down the floor, the nearest wing takes him at the rim rather than leaving him alone, and the defensive big, arriving last, takes whichever perimeter player is free. The defense has bought a protected rim at the cost of a size mismatch on the perimeter.
What the defense does about that mismatch is the subject of lecture 4.5, where the scram switch is the tool for getting a small defender out of the post and a big one in. For now the rule is simpler: fix the match-up on the next pass, not this one. A defense that tries to sort its assignments while the ball is live has stopped guarding to talk.






Assignment


Each defender takes the nearest unguarded attacker and calls the number. Mismatches are accepted now and fixed on the next pass.


Concedes


A mismatch somewhere on the floor, usually a small guard on a big or a big on a guard.


Requires


Talk. Five players who each say one number, once.


Beaten by


An offense that finds the mismatch before the defense fixes it: the early seal by a big on a small defender, or a guard attacking a big on the perimeter before the scram switch can happen.





Coverage 4: Match up: the third job, and the one where being wrong is allowed.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
text:
5 Before the shot goes up
Most of transition defense is decided before the possession changes, while the team is still on offense. The question is who goes to the offensive glass and who retreats, and it is the mirror of the crash or get back decision from lecture 3.1. Every player sent to the glass is a rebound the team might win and a defender it will not have. The rule most teams adopt is floor balance: one or two designated players, usually the guards and usually the ones furthest from the rim when the shot goes up, retreat as the shot is released, whatever happens to it. They are the first defenders back in Section 1, and they are back because they never went.
The other thing a defense can do before the break starts is make it start late. Jamming the rebounder is the nearest player staying on the defensive rebounder as he lands, with a hand up in the passing lane, and the next player denying the outlet man on the sideline. The outlet is thrown a second late, or thrown to the middle, or not thrown. A break that starts a second late meets the defense from Section 1 already in the paint, and the whole of lecture 3.1’s first three seconds have been taken away before the first dribble.

title: 4.1: Transition Defense
section: 6 The take foul, and what the rule book did to it
text:
6 The take foul, and what the rule book did to it
For a long time there was a fourth job available, cheaper than the other three. If the break could not be stopped, a defender could foul the ball-handler early, before the numbers advantage was used, and trade the breakaway for two free throws and a set defense behind them. This is the transition take foul. Teams did it because they judged two free throws, which can be missed, a better outcome than an uncontested layup, and because the foul bought the time to get all five defenders back for whatever followed.
The NBA changed the trade. Beginning with the 2022-23 season, the penalty is listed in two bullets: “The offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “The offensive team will retain possession of the ball.”1 The foul now costs the defense a free throw and the possession it was trying to save, so the trade it was making no longer exists. The card below shows the coverage as a diff of itself, before and after, in the way a second model is shown as a change to the first.






Assignment


A defender fouls the ball-handler early in the break, before the numbers advantage is used.


Concedes


Two free throws, then a set defense. One free throw, taken by the best shooter on the floor, and the offense keeps the ball.


Requires


Nothing but the decision. A reason to give up a free throw and the ball to prevent one shot, which is hard to find.


Beaten by


Nothing on the floor. The rule.





Coverage 5: The take foul before and after 2022-23: the same action, a different trade.



The idea to carry into lecture 3.2 is that the three jobs do not end when the ball is stopped. The defense that has protected the rim, stopped the ball and matched up is back, but it is back badly: cross-matched, with its big still arriving and its assignments improvised. Early offense is the offense’s attack on exactly that state, and it starts with the one player the defense in Section 4 could not account for, the trailer stepping into a ball screen.

title: 3.1: Transition Offense
text:
New terms introduced (15): Corner fill, Fast break, Hit-ahead pass, Leak out, Numbers advantage, Outlet pass, Pace, Points per possession, Push, Rim runner, Running the lanes, Secondary break, Trailer, Transition, Transition three. Diagrams: 4.
Transition is the right place to begin, for the same reason a possession begins there. Every possession starts with a change of possession, and for the first few seconds after it the defense is not a defense yet: it is five players running in the same direction, none of them where they will end up. Everything the half court teaches later is a way of manufacturing an advantage against a set defense. In transition the advantage is handed over for free, and the whole subject is how fast the offense can take it before it is withdrawn.
The size of the gift is measurable. In the data set behind Jordan Sperber’s analysis of tempo, “the average points per transition play is 1.04” and “the average points per half-court play is 0.87”, both from play-by-play since the 2010 season.1 Cleaning the Glass, whose definitions most public analysis now uses, treats the half court as “the least efficient of the contexts” for the plain reason that “the defense is set and in the best guarding position.”2 Nothing the offense can draw up in the half court is as good as arriving before that happens.
This lecture takes the break in the order it unfolds. Section 1 says what transition is and why it works. Section 2 covers the first three seconds: the rebound, the outlet, and the push. Section 3 gives the shape of the break, running the lanes and the rim run, and the read that decides a 3-on-2. Section 4 covers the trailer and the secondary break, where the break turns into early offense. Section 5 sets out the decisions a team has to make about transition before the game starts. Each action is written in a card with the same five slots, and each card’s last slot points at the coverage in lecture 4.1 that is built to stop it.

title: 3.1: Transition Offense
section: 1 What transition is, and why it works
text:
1 What transition is, and why it works
Transition is the part of a possession between the change of possession and the moment the defense is set. Cleaning the Glass defines it as “anything that occurs as the teams are switching sides of the court and all 5 defenders are not back and set in a normal guarding position.”3 The definition matters because it is about the defense, not the offense: a possession is in transition until the defense has ended it, however fast or slowly the offense is moving.
Three things are true of an unset defense, and each one is a separate advantage:

There are fewer of them. Some defenders are still behind the play, so for a moment the offense has more players in the front court. This is the numbers advantage, and it is the most obvious of the three.
Nobody has a man. Even when five defenders are back, they have not matched up. Two may be near one attacker and none near another. The offense does not need to be faster than the defense, only faster than the defense’s communication.
There is no rim protector home. The big is usually the last player back. Until he arrives, a drive meets nobody at the rim, and a rim runner arriving first has the paint to himself.

The fast break is the attempt to score on the first of these before the other two are fixed. Early offense, taught in lecture 3.2, is the attempt to score on the second and third after the first has gone. The line between them is where the numbers even out.

title: 3.1: Transition Offense
text:
2 The first three seconds
A break is won or lost before the ball crosses half court, and mostly before it has been dribbled at all.

The outlet
The outlet pass is the first pass after a defensive rebound, from the rebounder to a guard who has moved to the sideline at about the free-throw line extended. Its job is to take the ball out of the crowd under the rim and put it in the hands of a player facing the other basket. A rebounder who lands, turns and throws the outlet in one motion starts the break a full second before one who lands, looks and then throws, and a full second is the difference between a 3-on-2 and a 3-on-3.
The outlet has a target and a rule. The target is the sideline, not the middle: a guard waiting in the middle of the floor is surrounded, and a guard on the sideline has the whole floor on one side of him. The rule is that the outlet man must come to the ball, not wait for it. A pass thrown to a stationary player is a pass the defense can read.


The push
Push means advancing the ball at speed on every change of possession, by pass first and by dribble second. The order matters. A hit-ahead pass moves the ball forty feet in under a second; the fastest player alive covers that distance in two. A team that pushes with the pass makes the defense sprint to a spot the ball has already left.
The push after a made basket is where teams differ most, because it is where it costs the most effort. After a miss everyone runs; after a make the inbounder has to take the ball out of the net and the natural pace is a walk. Teams that push after makes are buying two things: a defense that never gets to jog back, and a fourth quarter in which the other team’s legs are gone. Pace is the measure of how much a team does this, and it is discussed in Section 5.






Setup


A defensive rebound. The outlet man has already moved to the sideline at the free-throw line extended; the wings have already turned to run.


Trigger


The rebounder’s feet touch the floor.


Read


Is the outlet man open on the sideline? If yes, throw it. If not, one dribble out of the crowd and look ahead for a hit-ahead.


Payoff


The ball in the front court with the defense still turning around.


Beaten by


Jamming the rebounder: pressure on the rebounder as he lands and a body on the outlet man, so the first pass is late or never thrown.





Action 1: The outlet and the push: the first pass decides whether there is a break at all.

title: 3.1: Transition Offense
text:
3 The shape of the break
Once the ball is moving, the break has a shape, and the shape is the same in every system because it comes from the geometry of the floor rather than from any coach.

Running the lanes
The two wings sprint the sidelines, as wide as the floor allows, all the way to the corners if nobody stops them. This is running the lanes, and the point of running wide is not to get the ball. It is to make the retreating defense choose. A defender sprinting back has one instinct, which is to run to the paint, and running the lanes wide means that every defender who follows that instinct has left a shooter alone on the sideline. The wings are not decoys; they are the reason the defense cannot be in two places.
The big runs the middle, straight down the lane line to the rim. This is the rim run, and it is the fastest way to put the third advantage from Section 1 to use. If the big arrives at the rim before a defender does, the ball-handler has a lob or a dump-off; if a defender goes with him, that defender is not on the ball, and the handler has the paint. Either way the rim run forces the first defender back to make the decision the offense wants him to make.
The fifth player is the trailer, who arrives last and is the subject of Section 4. Figure 1 shows all five.






Figure 1: Running the lanes. The wings run wide to the corners, the big runs the middle to the rim, the ball is pushed up the middle, and the trailer arrives last at the top. The two defenders back have to choose between the paint and the sidelines.









Setup


Change of possession. Wings on the sidelines, big in the middle, ball in a guard’s hands.


Trigger


The outlet or the hit-ahead.


Read


Where does the first defender back go? If to the paint, the wing he left is open; if to a wing, the rim runner is open.


Payoff


A layup for the rim runner, or a corner three for the wing the defense abandoned.


Beaten by


Protecting the rim first with two defenders in the paint before the ball reaches the free-throw line, and closing out to the corners from the inside.





Action 2: Running the lanes: the shape of every break.





The numbers break
When the offense reaches the front court with more players than the defense, it has a numbers advantage, and the way to use it is the same at every level of the game. The ball goes to the middle of the floor and stays there until a defender commits to it. The ball-handler does not decide in advance whom to pass to; he dribbles at the free-throw line and lets the defense choose for him. A defender who steps up to the ball has left a wing open. A defender who stays home on a wing has left the ball-handler a lane to the rim. The handler’s only job is to keep his eyes up and go where the defense is not (Figure 2).






Figure 2: A 3-on-2. The ball attacks the middle of the floor with a wing on each side. Both passes are live; whichever defender commits to the ball leaves a wing, and if neither commits the ball-handler has a layup.



Two rules turn a numbers advantage into points instead of a turnover. First, the ball stays in the middle; a ball-handler who drifts to one side has cut the floor in half and turned a 3-on-2 into a 2-on-2 with a spectator. Second, the wings stay wide until the last moment and then cut to the rim at an angle, so that the pass they receive is a pass they can finish without dribbling. A wing who comes toward the ball to help has brought his defender with him.






Setup


More attackers than defenders in the front court: 3-on-2, 2-on-1, 4-on-3.


Trigger


The ball reaches the middle of the floor with a wing on each side.


Read


Which defender commits to the ball? Pass to the wing he left. If nobody commits, keep going to the rim.


Payoff


A layup, or a free throw on the foul that stops it.


Beaten by


Tandem defense: two defenders in a line rather than side by side, so the front man takes the ball and the back man takes the first pass, and the middle is never open.





Action 3: The numbers break: let the defense choose, then go the other way.





Finishing, and not finishing
The break is over when it produces a shot or when the defense is set, and a good break is as much about the second as the first. The shots a break is for are the layup and the corner three, and a break that does not produce one of those in the first seconds should not be forced into a worse shot. It should flow, without stopping, into Section 4. The mistake to watch for is the contested pull-up from the elbow with three defenders back: it uses up the transition possession and gets the half-court shot anyway.
The transition three deserves a word of its own, because it is the shot the geometry of Section 3 sets up and the shot a retreating defense concedes first. A defender sprinting to the paint has, for a beat, left the arc. A wing who runs to his spot and stops, rather than continuing to the rim, is open for that beat. Whether a team takes that shot is a decision about its shooters, and it is one of the decisions in Section 5.

title: 3.1: Transition Offense
section: 4 The trailer and the secondary break
text:
4 The trailer and the secondary break
Suppose the defense has done its job: two defenders back in the paint, the wings picked up, the rim runner met at the block. The first four attackers are matched. The fifth is not, because he has not arrived yet. He is the trailer, usually the other big, and he comes up the middle of the floor after the play. Nobody has him, because the defender who should have him is the last man back and is still behind him (Figure 3).






Figure 3: The trailer. The first wave is matched, four on four. The trailing big arrives at the top with nobody assigned to him, and the ball is reversed to him: a swing to the weak side, a shot if he shoots, or a ball screen for the guard if he does not.



What the trailer does with the ball is the start of the secondary break: a scripted continuation that flows out of the primary break without a pause. The three things a trailer can do are the three things a big at the top of the floor can always do. He can shoot, if he is a shooter. He can reverse the ball to the weak side, which is a trailer flip and which moves the ball to the side the defense loaded away from. Or he can step straight into a ball screen for the guard, which is the drag screen, and which is the first action of lecture 3.2. The secondary break is where transition becomes early offense, and the seam between the two lectures is a big man arriving at the top of the key.






Setup


The primary break has been stopped. Four attackers matched; the trailing big still coming.


Trigger


The trailer crosses the arc at the top.


Read


Is anyone on him? If not, he catches and shoots or swings. If his defender has sprinted back, he screens the ball instead.


Payoff


A trailer three, a reversed ball against a loaded defense, or a drag screen before the big has settled.


Beaten by


The opposing big sprinting back with the trailer rather than settling in the paint, so the trailer arrives guarded. See cross-match in lecture 4.1 for how the defense buys time when he cannot.





Action 4: The trailer: the one player the defense has not counted.

title: 3.1: Transition Offense
section: 5 Decisions a team makes before the game
text:
5 Decisions a team makes before the game
The actions above are common to every team. What differs between teams is a small number of decisions about transition that a coaching staff makes once, in preseason, and then holds to.
Crash or get back. On every shot the offense takes, each player either goes to the offensive glass or retreats. Sending players to the glass wins offensive rebounds; sending them back stops the other team’s break. This is crash or get back, and it is a trade with no free answer. Most teams designate a floor balance rule, one or two players who are always back, and let the rest crash. The rule changes with who is on the floor and with who the opponent is.
Whether to leak. A leak out is a player leaving before the rebound is won, to get behind the defense for a long pass. When it works it is a layup with no defender within thirty feet. When it fails, the offense has lost a rebounder and, if the other team keeps the ball, the defense has lost a defender. Teams that leak do it with a designated player against a designated shooter, not as a habit.
The transition three. Whether the wings stop at the arc or continue to the rim is a decision about the roster. A team of shooters runs to spots; a team of finishers runs to the rim. The wrong rule for the personnel turns the best shot in the game into an average one.
How hard to push. Pace is the number of possessions a team plays per game, and a team chooses its pace by how hard it pushes, above all after makes. More possessions favors the better team, since more trials means less variance in the result, and shifts more of the game’s shots into the context where efficiency is highest.

Gap. This section should carry the league’s pace by season, so that “teams play faster than they did” is a number and not a feeling. title: 3.1: Transition Offense
text:
6 How transition is counted
Because transition is defined by the state of the defense and not by the clock, it cannot be read off a box score, and the public numbers come from play-by-play tagging. Cleaning the Glass’s rule is that transition starts at the beginning of a possession and ends once the defense is set,4 and its measure of a team’s transition offense is the points per possession of possessions that began in transition, compared against what an average team does on a possession that did not. Sperber’s 1.04 and 0.87 are points per play rather than per possession, a distinction that matters when a possession contains an offensive rebound and therefore more than one play.5 Both are ways of saying the same thing, and both are the reason a coach who cannot make his team faster will at least try to make it earlier.
The idea to carry into lecture 4.1 is that every advantage in this lecture is a deadline. The numbers advantage lasts until the defense gets back. The unmatched trailer lasts until his man arrives. The empty rim lasts until the big is home. The whole of transition defense is the attempt to make those deadlines arrive sooner, and it is taught in the same order the offense attacks them: rim first, then the ball, then the match-ups.
