title: 3.10: Spacing and Roles
text:
New terms introduced (23): 4-out 1-in, 5-out, Block, Center (5), Combo guard, Corner, Drive, Dunker spot, Elbow, Gap, Kick-out, Point forward, Point guard (1), Power forward (4), Shooting guard (2), Skip pass, Slot, Small forward (3), Spacing, Strong side, The paint, Top of the key, Wing. Diagrams: 6.
Eight lectures of actions have taken the floor for granted. This one is about the floor. Every action so far works only if the players who are not in it are standing in the right places, and “the right places” has a precise meaning: far enough apart that one defender cannot guard two of them. That is spacing, and it is the quietest thing in basketball and the one that decides most possessions.
The lecture is mostly vocabulary, because a viewer needs the names of the spots before the rest of the site’s sentences mean anything. Section 1 names the floor: the areas and the spots. Section 2 is the alignments, 5-out and 4-out 1-in, and what each buys. Section 3 is the gap, the single measurement that explains why spacing matters. Section 4 is the three things that happen when spacing works: the drive, the kick-out and the skip pass. Section 5 is the five roles as they are actually played now.

title: 3.10: Spacing and Roles
text:
1 The floor
Split the court lengthwise, basket to basket, and the half the ball is on is the strong side; the other is the weak side, which on defense is where help comes from. That is the first division every player learns, and half the defensive vocabulary of Chapter 4 refers to it.
The painted rectangle from the baseline to the free-throw line is the paint, also called the key or the lane. Inside it, against the rim, is the restricted area, the half-circle inside which a secondary defender cannot draw a charge. The painted marks on the lane lines nearest the baseline are the blocks, and the traditional post-up spot is on one of them. Where the free-throw line meets a lane line is an elbow, the hub of high-post play and the spot the two bigs stand on in Horns. The middle of the free-throw line is the nail, which is a defensive spot: it is where a help defender stands to threaten a drive from either side, taught in lecture 4.4.
Outside the arc, going round from the baseline: the corner, where the three-point line meets the sideline and the shot is shortest; the wing, level with the free-throw line extended; the slot, above the arc roughly in line with the lane line; and the top of the key, straight out from the rim. Between the corner and the block, just outside the lane, is the dunker spot, where a non-shooting big waits for lobs and drop-offs, and where the hammer of lecture 3.6 sends its screener.

title: 3.10: Spacing and Roles
text:
2 The alignments
A team’s alignment is how many players stand outside the arc. 5-out puts all five outside it, as in Figure 1, and the paint is empty: any drive meets nobody until a defender leaves his man. It is the base of the delay offense of lecture 3.2 and of most modern motion. It asks one thing of a roster, which is that all five players can be guarded outside the arc; a non-shooting big standing at the arc is guarded by a defender who simply stands in the lane, which turns 5-out into 4-out with an extra defender in the paint.






Figure 1: 5-out. Every attacker outside the arc, so every defender is too, and a drive from the top meets nobody until someone leaves his man.



4-out 1-in puts four outside and one inside, usually in the dunker spot rather than on the block, as in Figure 2. It concedes one defender in the paint and gains a drop-off target and an offensive rebounder. Which alignment a team uses is a roster decision in the same way the systems of lecture 3.9 are.






Figure 2: 4-out 1-in. The one inside player waits in the dunker spot; his defender is the only one in the paint, and he has to decide whether to leave it when the drive comes.

title: 3.10: Spacing and Roles
text:
3 The gap
A gap is the distance between two attackers on the perimeter, measured in spots. If they are in neighboring spots, slot and wing, that is a single gap. If the spot between them is empty, slot and corner with the wing vacant, that is a double gap, as in Figure 3. The difference decides whether a drive is worth attempting: driving a single gap means the second defender is one step away, and driving a double gap means he is two, which is the difference between help arriving before the driver and after him.






Figure 3: Gap. On the right, two attackers one spot apart: a single gap. On the left, the wing is empty, so the slot and the corner make a double gap, and that is where the drive goes.



This is what spacing means, operationally. It is not “stand far apart”; it is “stand so that the gaps the ball can attack are double, and so that no defender can guard two attackers at once.” Every offense in this chapter creates double gaps somewhere. Dribble drive motion is built on nothing else.

title: 3.10: Spacing and Roles
text:
4 Drive, kick-out, skip
Three things happen when the spacing is right, and they follow one another.
The drive is the ball-handler beating his man into the gap, as in Figure 4. A drive is not primarily a way to score; it is a way to make two defenders guard one player, which is the same thing a ball screen does, achieved without a screen. Once the second defender commits, the driver is no longer looking at the rim, he is looking at the man that defender left.






Figure 4: The drive. The handler attacks the double gap. The nail defender steps across and the weak-side defender sinks; both of their men are now open, which is what the drive was for.



The kick-out is the pass to that man, as in Figure 5. It is the most common assist in the modern game, because the modern floor puts a shooter in each corner and the modern defense sends help from one of them.






Figure 5: The kick-out. The weak-side defender has helped at the rim; the driver passes out to the man he left, and if that defender recovers, the shooter swings it on to the corner.



The skip pass is the longer version, thrown across the floor over the defense rather than around it, as in Figure 6. It skips the players in between, which is where the name comes from, and it is thrown when the whole defense has shifted to one side: the recovery is then a closeout from the middle of the paint to the far corner, which is the longest closeout in the game and the one that produces the most open shots.






Figure 6: The skip pass. The defense has shifted to the ball; the pass goes across the floor to the far corner, and the closeout that has to cover it starts in the paint.









Setup


A handler with a live dribble facing a double gap, two shooters spaced on the weak side, and either an empty paint or a big in the dunker spot.


Trigger


The handler’s defender is beaten or leaning, and the gap is two spots wide.


Read


The driver reads the second defender, not the rim. Nobody helps: finish. The nail defender steps across: the shooter behind him is open at the top or the far slot. The low man helps at the rim: the corner he left is open. The big’s defender leaves the dunker spot: the drop-off. If the defense recovers before the pass, the ball is swung on and the next player attacks the gap that has opened.


Payoff


A layup, or the open shot belonging to whichever defender chose to help.


Beaten by


Guarding the drive with one defender, which needs a player who can stay in front; a stunt that fakes help and recovers; or building a wall in the middle and conceding the pull-up. All in lecture 4.4.





Action 1: The drive, the kick-out and the skip pass: one action that makes two defenders guard one player, and the two passes that punish whichever one comes.

title: 3.10: Spacing and Roles
text:
5 The five roles
The numbers are still used, and still mean something, but what each number does has changed enough that the old definitions mislead.
The point guard, the 1, is the primary ball-handler and initiator. The shooting guard, the 2, is the secondary handler and perimeter scorer, today mostly an off-ball mover who comes off the screens of lectures 3.5 and 3.6. The small forward, the 3, is the wing, expected to shoot, drive and guard several positions. The power forward, the 4, was the second post player and is now often a perimeter player who screens, pops and makes the short-roll decisions of lecture 3.3; when he shoots from the arc he is called a stretch four. The center, the 5, is the primary screener, roller and rim protector.
Two role names exist because the numbers stopped fitting. A combo guard moves between initiating and spacing without a fixed role. A point forward is a forward-sized player who runs the offense, which puts a bigger, slower defender at the point of attack and is a mismatch before anything has happened.
The reason the roles matter for this chapter is that every system in lecture 3.9 is chosen for the players on the roster, and every action in lectures 3.2 to 3.8 is run for a particular kind of player. A ball screen for a point forward is a different action from a ball screen for a point guard, even though the diagram is identical.
The idea to carry into lecture 3.11 is that spacing, gaps and roles are the raw material of an offense that has no script at all. The next lecture is about those: motion, read and react, isolation and the mismatch, and how an offense chooses the action that beats the coverage it is being shown.

title: 3.8: Sets and Systems
text:
New terms introduced (3): Horns, Set play, Zipper. Diagrams: 2.
Five lectures of actions have treated each action as a thing on its own. A team does not run one action; it starts from a shape and runs a sequence. The shape is the set, and the sequence is the play. This lecture is about both, and about the difference, because the two words are used interchangeably on a broadcast and mean different things.
A set is where the five players stand when the possession starts: Horns with two bigs at the elbows, 5-out with everyone outside the arc, a box with four players in a square. It carries no instructions. What it does is decide which actions are available and which help is far away, and a good set makes several different plays look identical for the first two seconds.
A set play is the script: this screen, then that cut, then this pass, run to get one shot for one player. It is the opposite of the motion offense and flow of lecture 3.11, which give players rules instead of a script.
Section 1 is Horns, the most common set in the sport and the clearest example of what a set is for. Section 2 is Zipper, an action named for the cut it contains, which teams run out of several sets. Section 3 is the set play as a concept: why teams run them, when, and what they cost. Section 4 names the sets and plays heard on a broadcast for which this site has a description but not an entry.

title: 3.8: Sets and Systems
text:
1 Horns
Horns is the point guard at the top with the ball, two bigs at the two elbows, and two shooters in the two corners, as in Figure 1. Every glossary that names it names the same shape. What it buys is stated by looking at the floor: the paint is empty, so any drive meets nobody; the two bigs are both a pass away from the ball and both able to screen it; the two shooters are in the corners, the furthest a help defender can be from the rim and still be guarding someone who can shoot.






Figure 1: Horns. The ball at the top, two bigs at the elbows, two shooters in the corners, the paint empty. This is the alignment, not a play; a dozen plays start from it.



From that shape, several plays start the same way and end differently. Figure 2 shows one of them: the ball-handler takes a ball screen from one big and drives away from it, while the other big, instead of rolling, sets a flare screen for the corner shooter lifting to the wing, and the skip pass goes there. The first two seconds are identical to a plain pick-and-roll, and the defense has to guard both.






Figure 2: One play from Horns. The handler takes the ball screen from the right elbow and drives left; the left-elbow big flares for the shooter lifting from the corner; the skip pass goes to the wing while the screener rolls.









Setup


The handler at the top with the ball. Two bigs at the elbows, facing him. Two shooters in the corners. The paint empty.


Trigger


The handler picks a side: he dribbles at one elbow, which turns that big into a screener and the other into an off-ball threat.


Read


The handler reads which big’s defender commits. If the screener’s defender plays the ball, the screener rolls into an empty paint. If the defense switches, the rolling big has a mismatch and the early seal of lecture 3.7 is on. If the weak-side defenders shade toward the ball screen, the second big’s flare or pin-down for a corner shooter is open, and the pass is a skip. If the corners’ defenders never leave, the ball screen is two-on-two with the whole paint to work in.


Payoff


A pick-and-roll with no help in the lane and a weak-side action running at the same time, from a shape that makes several plays look the same at the start.


Beaten by


Switching everything, which takes away the screens and concedes the mismatches; or a big who plays the ball screen at the level while the low man tags the roller. Lecture 4.3, lecture 4.4 and lecture 4.5.





Action 1: Horns: a shape that empties the paint and puts two screeners a pass away.

title: 3.8: Sets and Systems
text:
2 Zipper
The zipper is an action rather than a set: a player cuts from the block straight up the lane line off a screen and catches at the slot, as in Figure 3. It is a pin-down with the cut made vertically along the lane line rather than out toward the wing, and what it buys is a catch at the top with the whole floor in front of the catcher rather than a catch on the wing with half of it. Teams run it as the first action of a possession, to get the ball into the hands of a guard who did not bring it up, and as an entry into a ball screen: the catcher at the slot is immediately in position for the big to screen for him.






Figure 3: Zipper. The guard cuts from the block straight up the lane line off the big’s screen and catches at the slot, with the floor in front of him.









Setup


The ball at the top or the wing. A guard on the block. A big on the lane line above him, facing the baseline. The weak side spaced.


Trigger


The screen is set on the lane line; the guard cuts.


Read


The four reads of lecture 3.5 apply: chased over, curl to the rim; defender under, catch at the slot and shoot; caught, straight up and catch; jumped above, back cut. The screener reads his own defender: if he helps on the cut, slip to the rim.


Payoff


A guard catching at the slot with the floor in front of him, usually straight into a ball screen from the man who just screened for him.


Beaten by


Top-locking the cutter so he cannot come up the lane line, conceding the back cut; or switching the screen. Lecture 4.4 and lecture 4.5.





Action 2: Zipper: up the lane line to the slot, with the floor in front.

title: 3.8: Sets and Systems
text:
3 The set play
A set play is a script. Its value is that five players know what is coming and the defense does not, and its cost is that it takes three or four seconds to set up, during which the defense is getting organized. That trade decides when teams run them: after a timeout, when the defense cannot have prepared for this one; at the start of a possession against a set defense, when nothing is available anyway; for a specific player who needs a specific shot; and at the end of a quarter or a game, when there is one possession and no second chance. The rest of the time most teams would rather play with rules, which is lecture 3.11.






Setup


A named alignment (Horns, box, 1-4, double stack) and five players who know the script.


Trigger


A call, a hand signal, or a dead ball. An ATO is the standard case, taught in lecture 3.12.


Read


A set play is not read-free. Every good one has an option at each beat: if the first cutter is covered, the second screen is the answer; if the defense switches, the mismatch is the answer. What distinguishes it from motion is that the options are enumerated in advance rather than derived from rules.


Payoff


One specific shot for one specific player against a defense that has not seen this sequence today.


Beaten by


A defense that has scouted the set and jumps the first action, which is why teams run several plays that look identical for two seconds; and by the clock, since a play that takes four seconds to set up leaves fewer to improvise with if it fails.





Action 3: The set play: a script, worth its cost when the defense cannot have prepared for it.

title: 3.8: Sets and Systems
section: 4 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
text:
4 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
The sets and plays below are named by one publisher, or are one team’s call for an action this site already teaches under another name. Each has a description here and no entry; the rule and the dated diff are in data/sources/glossary_diff_2026-09-21.md.

Horns twist. A Horns play in which the two elbow bigs screen for each other before one of them screens the ball, so the ball screen arrives from the side the defense did not expect.
1-4 set, box set, double stack. Three more alignments. The 1-4 has both bigs at the elbows and both wings in the corners, which flattens the defense and opens the lane for back cuts; the box is four players in a square at the elbows and blocks; the double stack puts two players on each block. Box and stack are taught in lecture 3.12, where they are used most.
Miami. A combination in which the ball is entered to the high post, the point guard sets a shuffle screen, and the shuffle screener then takes a handoff from the high post.
Corner offense. An alignment with three players on the strong side (a big at the elbow, a guard in the corner and one on the wing), a big at the weak-side elbow, and a forward near the weak-side slot.
Team-named plays. The plays pages of the coaching sites are full of calls named for teams and colleges. Those are one team’s name for a sequence, not vocabulary, and they are out of scope for this site by rule.

The idea to carry into lecture 3.9 is that a set play ends. The offenses in the next lecture do not: they are continuities, which return to their own starting shape and can be run until the shot clock ends.

title: 3.3: On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family
text:
New terms introduced (9): 4-on-3, Lob, Pick-and-roll, Pop, Roll, Screen, Short roll, Snake dribble, Step-up screen. Diagrams: 6.
Everything in lecture 3.2 got the ball to a moving player past a defender who was not yet set. Against a defense that is set, the offense has to make that seam itself, and the tool it uses most is the screen: one attacker stands still in the path a defender needs to take, so that for one step the defender cannot go where his man is going. Set for the player with the ball, it is a ball screen, and a ball screen followed by the screener running to the rim is the pick-and-roll. It is the most common action in the sport at every level, and the sentence on the front page of this site (“they iced the drag and the low man tagged, so 5 short-rolled”) is a description of one.
The pick-and-roll works because it puts two defenders in a position where two things are true at once. The ball-handler’s defender has been screened and is now behind the ball. The screener’s defender therefore has to help on the ball, and the moment he does, the screener rolling behind him is unguarded. Two defenders, two threats, and one of them is going to be late. Every coverage in lecture 4.3 is a different answer to which one, and every action in this lecture is a way of punishing the answer.
Section 1 defines the screen and the base action. Section 2 is the screener’s three choices after the screen: the roll, the pop, and the short roll. Section 3 is two ways the ball-handler changes the geometry: the step-up screen and the snake dribble. Section 4 is the 4-on-3, which is what the offense has when the defense sends two defenders at the ball. Each action is a card, and each card’s last slot names the coverage built to stop it.

title: 3.3: On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family
section: 1 The screen and the base action
text:
1 The screen and the base action
A screen is legal when the screener is stationary and inside his own cylinder when contact comes; the moment he leans or steps into the defender it is a foul. Because he has to stand still, the whole art of screening is where he stands and at what angle: a screen set a foot too high lets the defender go under it, a foot too low lets him go over. The angle of the screen decides which way the ball-handler can go, and the defense reads that angle before the ball moves.
The base pick-and-roll is shown in Figure 1. The screener arrives, the handler comes off the screen toward the middle, the screener rolls. What the screener’s defender does here decides everything: in the figure he has dropped back toward the free-throw line, which is the drop coverage of lecture 4.3.






Figure 1: The pick-and-roll against a drop. The big screens the handler’s defender; the handler comes off toward the middle; the big rolls to the rim. The big’s defender has dropped to the free-throw line to meet the handler, which is what leaves the roller open behind him.









Setup


The ball-handler above the arc at the slot or the wing with a live dribble. The screener at the elbow or the top. The other three spaced so the lane is empty: two corners and a weak-side wing, or two corners and the dunker spot.


Trigger


The screener arrives and sets his feet on the handler’s defender’s shoulder, angled so the handler can go toward the middle.


Read


The handler comes off the screen and reads the screener’s defender. Dropped back: pull up at the elbow, or drive at him and pass to the roller if he commits. Stepped up to the ball: hit the roller behind him. Switched onto the handler: attack the big off the dribble, or find the screener sealing the smaller defender. Two defenders on the ball: pass out to the short roll and play 4-on-3.


Payoff


The handler with a defender behind him rather than in front, a big rolling to the rim, and a defense that has to choose which one to guard.


Beaten by


Any of the coverages of lecture 4.3 played well; the base answer is the drop, which concedes a mid-range pull-up to take away the roll and the drive.





Action 1: The pick-and-roll: a screen for the ball, then a roll, and two defenders who cannot both be right.
crumbs: 3.3: On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family

title: 3.3: On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family
text:
2 The screener’s three choices
After the screen the screener does one of three things, and which one is decided by who he is and what the defense did.
The roll is the base: turn toward the rim as the handler comes off, run to the block, and catch a pass or a lob at the rim. A rolling big who can catch and finish above the rim changes the coverage the defense can play, because a drop that stays at the free-throw line concedes the lob every time.
The pop is the roll’s opposite. A screener who can shoot steps out to the arc instead of rolling, as in Figure 2, and the pass comes back out to him. It is the pick-and-pop. It punishes the drop, because the dropping defender is at the free-throw line guarding a drive that never comes while his man shoots a three above him. The card below is written as a diff of the base action: the slots that change are marked with what was and what is now.






Figure 2: The pick-and-pop. The same screen; the screener steps out to the arc instead of rolling. The dropping defender is guarding the paint while his man is at the three-point line.









Setup


As the pick-and-roll, with a screener who can shoot from the arc.


Trigger


The screen, and the screener’s defender dropping toward the rim.


Read


The handler reads the dropping defender and passes to the roller behind him. The handler comes off the screen, draws the drop one more step, and passes back out to the screener at the arc.


Payoff


A roll to the rim. An open three for a big, or a drop defender who has to leave the paint to contest it, which reopens the drive.


Beaten by


A coverage that keeps the screener’s defender attached to him, which is to switch the screen or to play it at the level, both in lecture 4.3.





Action 2: The pick-and-pop as a diff of the pick-and-roll: the screener’s cut reverses, and the defense’s drop becomes a mistake.



The short roll is the roll that stops early. When the defense sends two defenders at the ball, a blitz in the vocabulary of lecture 4.3, the screener rolls only as far as the free-throw line, catches the pass out of the trap, and now has the ball facing three defenders with three teammates, as in Figure 3. He is not trying to score from there. He is a passer, and the possession has become the 4-on-3 of Section 4.






Figure 3: The short roll. Two defenders trap the handler. The screener rolls to the free-throw line, catches, and plays 4-on-3 against the three defenders who did not trap: a shooter in each corner, a cutter at the dunker spot, and his own drive.









Setup


As the pick-and-roll, against a defense that traps the ball screen. The two corners filled by shooters; the fourth attacker in the weak-side dunker spot.


Trigger


The screener’s defender jumps out to trap the handler with the handler’s own defender.


Read


The screener rolls to the free-throw line and shows his hands. The handler gets the ball out of the trap to him. The screener reads the three remaining defenders: the low man on the weak side is the one who has to choose between the dunker spot and the corner, and the pass goes to whichever he leaves.


Payoff


A big with the ball at the free-throw line, three defenders to beat, and three teammates open somewhere.


Beaten by


The trap arriving so fast that the pass out is a turnover, or a low man good enough to guard two players for a second, which is the X-out rotation of lecture 4.4.





Action 3: The short roll: against a trap, stop at the free-throw line and pass.

title: 3.3: On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family
section: 3 Changing the geometry: the step-up and the snake
text:
3 Changing the geometry: the step-up and the snake
The step-up screen changes where the screen sends the ball. In the base action the screener stands so the handler goes toward the middle. In a step-up the screener sets the screen with his back to the baseline, below the handler’s defender, so the handler comes off going toward the baseline and the rim, as in Figure 4. Defenses that want to force everything toward the sideline, the ice coverage of lecture 4.3, are built for a screen that comes from above; a step-up comes from below and sends the handler exactly where ice wanted him not to go.






Figure 4: The step-up screen. The screener stands below the handler’s defender with his back to the baseline. The handler comes off toward the baseline and the rim; the screener pops or re-screens.









Setup


The handler on the wing with the ball. The screener arrives from the block or the dunker spot rather than from the top.


Trigger


The screener plants below the handler’s defender, facing the handler, back to the baseline.


Read


The handler comes off toward the baseline. If his defender fights over, the handler is going downhill along the baseline against the big alone. If the defender goes under, the handler stops and shoots. If the big steps out to help, the screener pops toward the wing or re-screens the other way.


Payoff


A drive toward the baseline against a defense whose rules were written for a drive toward the middle.


Beaten by


Switching it, or a big who plays it at the level and turns the handler back toward the middle, where the help is. Both in lecture 4.3.





Action 4: The step-up screen: the same screen from below, and the defense’s sideline rule turned against it.



The snake dribble changes where the handler goes after the screen. He comes off toward the middle as usual, but instead of continuing he cuts back across in front of the defender who is chasing him, so that defender ends up on his back, as in Figure 5. The dropping big now has to guard the handler alone, and the roller is coming down the other side of the lane. It is a two-on-one with the trailing defender taken out of it.






Figure 5: The snake dribble. The handler comes off the screen toward the middle, then cuts back across the trailing defender’s path, keeping him on his back. The dropping big is alone against the handler while the screener rolls down the far side of the lane.









Setup


The base pick-and-roll against a drop, with the handler’s defender fighting over the screen and chasing.


Trigger


The handler feels the chaser on his hip and the dropping big level with the free-throw line.


Read


The handler snakes back across the chaser’s path. The chaser is now behind him and cannot recover without fouling. The handler reads the big: if the big stays back, pull up; if he steps up, the roller is behind him; if he stays with the roller, drive.


Payoff


The handler alone against the big with the chaser removed, and the roller open on the far side.


Beaten by


The chaser going under the screen rather than over, so there is no one to snake in front of; or the big playing at the level so the handler has no room to change direction. Lecture 4.3.





Action 5: The snake dribble: the handler takes his own defender out of the play.
crumbs: 3.3: On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family

title: 3.3: On-Ball Screens I: The Pick-and-Roll Family
text:
4 The 4-on-3
When the defense sends two defenders at the ball, it has chosen to guard the other four attackers with three. That is the 4-on-3, and it is the geometry every trapping coverage has to live with. Figure 6 shows it: the ball is trapped at the slot, the short-rolling big is at the free-throw line, a shooter is in each corner, and the fourth attacker is in the dunker spot. The three remaining defenders form a triangle and cannot cover all four.






Figure 6: 4-on-3. Two defenders on the ball at the slot. The other three guard the big at the free-throw line, two corner shooters and the dunker spot, and cannot cover all four. The pass out of the trap starts the count.









Setup


A ball screen that the defense has trapped. The short-roller at the free-throw line; shooters in both corners; the fourth attacker in the weak-side dunker spot.


Trigger


The pass out of the trap.


Read


The receiver reads the three defenders. The weak-side low man is the key: he cannot guard the dunker spot and the weak corner at once. If he sinks to the dunker, the corner is open; if he stays with the corner, the dunker is open for a lob or a drop-off; if the nail defender comes to the ball, the strong corner is open.


Payoff


A layup or a corner three, chosen by which defender the defense left short.


Beaten by


Rotations fast enough to cover four spots with three men for the two seconds it takes the trap to recover, which is the whole of lecture 4.4, and a trap that gets the ball out of the handler’s hands late enough that the shot clock does the rest.





Action 6: The 4-on-3: what the defense hands over when it sends two at the ball.



The idea to carry into lecture 3.4 is that every action here is the pick-and-roll with one variable changed: who the screener is, which way the screen faces, what the screener does after, where the handler goes. The named actions in the next lecture change more than one at a time, and most of them exist because the coverages in Chapter 4 got good at guarding the version with one.

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
text:
New terms introduced (6): Back screen, Cross screen, Flare screen, Pin-down, Rip screen, Stagger. Diagrams: 6.
A ball screen frees the player who already has the ball. An off-ball screen frees the player who is about to get it, and that is a different problem, because the defense is not watching him. A defender guarding a player without the ball stands between his man and the ball, with his head turned to see both, and everything about an off-ball screen is designed around where that defender is looking. A screen he can see coming, he can avoid. A screen set on his blind side, or set while he is turned toward the ball, he cannot.
The six screens in this lecture are the shapes. What distinguishes them is the direction the screen faces and the direction the cutter goes: up toward the perimeter, away along the arc, back toward the rim, across the lane. The named actions of lecture 3.6 are built by combining two or three of these; this lecture is the parts list. Section 1 is the pin-down and the four reads a cutter makes off it, which are the same four reads off every screen here. Section 2 is the flare screen, for a defender who cheats toward the ball. Section 3 is the back screen and the rip screen, both set behind a defender who is watching the ball. Section 4 is the cross screen, the big man’s screen. Section 5 is the stagger, two screens for one cutter.
crumbs: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
section: 1 The pin-down, and the four reads
text:
1 The pin-down, and the four reads
The pin-down is the most common off-ball screen in the sport, and the one every shooter learns first. A shooter starts near the baseline, usually on the block or in the corner. A screener stands above him, facing the baseline, and the shooter runs up off the screen to the wing or the slot for a catch, as in Figure 1. It is also called a down screen, because the screener has come down toward the baseline to set it.






Figure 1: The pin-down. The screener faces the baseline; the shooter starts near the block and runs up off the screen to the wing. His defender, who was between him and the perimeter, has to go around the screen to follow him.



What makes the pin-down teachable is that the cutter has the same four choices off it that he has off every off-ball screen, and the choice is decided by what his defender does:

Curl. The defender chases the cutter over the top of the screen, right behind him. The cutter curls the screen, turning it into a cut toward the rim, and the defender is trailing.
Fade. The defender goes under the screen, between the screener and the rim, to meet the cutter at the wing. The cutter fades the other way, away from the ball toward the corner, and the defender has gone the wrong side of the screen.
Straight cut. The defender is caught on the screen. The cutter comes straight up to the wing and shoots.
Back cut. The defender anticipates and jumps above the screen to deny the catch at the wing. The cutter reverses and goes back door to the rim behind him, the back cut of lecture 3.7.







Setup


The shooter on the block or in the corner, his defender between him and the perimeter. The screener above him, facing the baseline. The ball on the other side of the floor or at the top, in the hands of a passer who can see the wing.


Trigger


The screener sets his feet. The shooter waits until the screen is set, then runs; a cutter who leaves early runs past his own screen.


Read


The shooter reads his defender against the screen: chasing over, curl; going under, fade; caught, straight cut and shoot; jumping above, back cut. The passer reads the same thing one beat later and delivers the ball to the spot the read chose.


Payoff


A shooter catching on the perimeter with his defender behind the screen, or a layup for the cutter who curled or back cut.


Beaten by


Top-locking the shooter: his defender stands above him, between him and the screen, and refuses to let him get to it, conceding the back cut to take away the shot. Taught in lecture 4.4. The other answer is to switch the screen, lecture 4.5.





Action 1: The pin-down: the screen a shooter learns first, and the four reads he makes off every screen after it.



Two names heard for versions of the pin-down have no entry of their own on this site. A wide pin-down is set in the corner or the short corner for a cutter who starts in the corner, so the cut is longer and the catch is at the wing. A double screen is two screeners standing shoulder to shoulder so the cutter’s defender has to go round both; when they are one behind the other instead of side by side, it is the stagger of Section 5. A chin is a back screen set in the slot, on one glossary’s description; another describes it as that back screen followed by a flare for the other slot player, and until the two agree the word has a description here and not a card.
crumbs: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
text:
2 The flare screen
The flare screen is for the defender who cheats toward the ball. A perimeter player is standing at the top or the slot, and his defender, watching the ball on the wing, has drifted a step toward it. A screener steps into the path the defender would take to follow his man away from the ball, and the man fades along the arc to the far wing, as in Figure 2. The pass is a skip pass over the top. The flare is the pin-down turned ninety degrees: the cutter goes sideways along the arc rather than up from the baseline, and the screen is set on the side of the defender that faces away from the ball.






Figure 2: The flare screen. The defender at the top has cheated toward the ball. The screener steps into the path he would take to follow his man, and the man fades along the arc to the far wing for a skip pass.









Setup


The ball on one wing. A shooter at the top or the far slot whose defender is shading toward the ball. A screener, usually a big, at the elbow or the slot on the shooter’s far side.


Trigger


The shooter’s defender takes his step toward the ball, or turns his head to it.


Read


The screener steps into the defender’s recovery path and the shooter fades away from the ball. The passer on the wing reads the defender: caught on the flare, skip the ball to the shooter; going under the flare toward the rim, the shooter lifts higher along the arc for the same pass; switched, the screener has a smaller defender at the elbow and seals him for an entry.


Payoff


An open three on the weak side, thrown over a defense that was leaning the other way.


Beaten by


A defender who stays on the line between his man and the ball and never cheats, which costs the defense its help on the drive; or a switch. Lecture 4.4 and lecture 4.5.





Action 2: The flare screen: the cutter goes away from the ball, and the defender who leaned toward it is screened.
crumbs: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
section: 3 The back screen and the rip
text:
3 The back screen and the rip
The back screen is set where the defender cannot see it. A defender guarding a player away from the ball stands between him and the ball, facing the ball. The screener comes up behind that defender and sets the screen on his back, and the man he is guarding cuts to the rim, as in Figure 3. The defender learns about the screen when he tries to follow his man and cannot. The pass is a lob or a bounce pass to the block. The UCLA cut of lecture 3.7 is a back screen set at the elbow; the Spain pick-and-roll of lecture 3.4 is a back screen set on the roller’s defender.






Figure 3: The back screen. The defender at the slot is facing the ball. The screener sets the screen on his back, and the slot player cuts to the rim. The pass is a lob or a bounce pass to the block.









Setup


The ball on one wing. A player at the far slot or the top, his defender between him and the ball with his back to the elbow. A screener at the elbow or the free-throw line behind that defender.


Trigger


The defender turns his head to the ball.


Read


The screener sets his feet on the defender’s back. The cutter goes to the rim on the side away from the screen. The passer reads the defender: screened, the lob; slipped under to the rim, the cutter pops out to the arc where the defender was, for a three; switched, the screener has the smaller defender and seals for a post catch.


Payoff


A cutter at the rim with his defender behind a screen he did not see.


Beaten by


The defender feeling the screen coming and going under it toward the rim early, conceding the pop; or a defense that switches every back screen, so the big’s defender takes the cutter and the guard’s defender takes the big. Lecture 4.5.





Action 3: The back screen: set on a defender’s back while he is watching the ball.



The rip screen is a back screen with a particular cutter: the player who has just set a screen himself. A big sets a pin-down or a ball screen; his defender is now above him toward the ball, having helped on the cutter; a second player comes across and back-screens that defender, and the big rips to the rim, as in Figure 4. It is the simplest form of screening the screener, and it works because a defender who has just helped on a screen is standing exactly where a back screen wants him.






Figure 4: The rip screen. The big at the elbow has just set a down screen and his defender is above him toward the ball. A second player comes across the lane and back-screens that defender; the big rips to the rim.









Setup


A big who has just set a screen at the elbow or the wing, with his defender above him toward the ball. A second attacker on the far block, ready to come across.


Trigger


The big’s defender helps on the first cutter and is a step above the big.


Read


The second attacker screens the big’s defender from behind. The big cuts to the rim. The passer reads the big’s defender: screened, the pass to the rim; recovering under, the big seals him and the pass is a post entry; the rip screener’s defender switching to the big, the rip screener himself is open where he set the screen.


Payoff


A big at the rim whose defender was screened while he was doing his job on the first screen.


Beaten by


The big’s defender never leaving the big to help on the first screen, which is what the drop coverage of lecture 4.3 buys; or a switch. Lecture 4.5.





Action 4: The rip screen: a back screen for the man who just screened.
crumbs: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
text:
4 The cross screen
The cross screen is set across the lane, block to block, and it is the screen that gets a big man a post catch. Two bigs are on the two blocks; one comes across and screens the other’s defender; the other cuts across the lane to the ball-side block, seals his man, and catches the entry pass, as in Figure 5. The ball usually arrives by reversal: it is on the far wing when the screen is set and comes to the near wing as the cutter arrives. Because the screen is set low, the cutter’s defender has to choose between going over it, which puts him behind the cutter, and going under it, which puts him under the rim and out of the passing lane.






Figure 5: The cross screen. One big comes across the lane and screens the other’s defender; the other cuts block to block, seals, and catches the entry pass as the ball arrives on the near wing.









Setup


Two bigs on the two blocks. The ball on the far wing, about to be reversed toward the cutter’s destination.


Trigger


The reversal pass leaves the far wing.


Read


The screener crosses the lane and sets the screen on the cutter’s defender; the cutter comes across and seals. The passer on the near wing reads the defender: over the top and behind the cutter, feed the post; under the screen, the cutter steps to the elbow for a face-up catch; switched, the screener now has the smaller defender on the far block and the pass goes to him instead, which is the screen-the-screener idea again.


Payoff


A post catch on the block for a big who has his defender sealed on his back.


Beaten by


The cutter’s defender going over the top and getting to the block first, then fronting the post; or a low man who bumps the cutter as he crosses the lane. Lecture 4.4.





Action 5: The cross screen: block to block, across the lane, for a post catch.
crumbs: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types

title: 3.5: Off-Ball Screens I: The Screen Types
text:
5 The stagger
The stagger is two screens in a row in the same direction for one cutter, as in Figure 6. Two screeners stand one above the other along the cutter’s path, and the cutter runs off both. The defender has to get around two bodies rather than one, and if he chooses the wrong side of the first screen he is on the wrong side of the second. The stagger is the base of most of the named off-ball actions in lecture 3.6: the floppy is a single screen one way and a stagger the other, the loop is a stagger along the baseline.






Figure 6: The stagger. Two screeners in a line, the second a few feet above the first. The shooter runs up off both from the corner to the slot; his defender has to get around two bodies.









Setup


The shooter in the corner or on the block. Two screeners along his path to the slot, the second a step above and inside the first, both facing the direction the shooter comes from. The ball on the other side.


Trigger


Both screens set; the shooter runs.


Read


The four reads apply at each screen. The common one: the defender chases over the first screen, so the shooter curls the second; or the defender goes under the first to beat the shooter to the second, so the shooter fades off the first back toward the corner. The second screener also reads: if his own defender jumps out to the shooter, the second screener slips to the rim.


Payoff


A shooter catching at the slot with his defender two screens behind, or a slip to the rim by the second screener.


Beaten by


The shooter’s defender going under both screens and meeting him at the catch, which concedes a curl; or switching the second screen, so the second screener’s defender takes the shooter. Lecture 4.5.





Action 6: The stagger: two screens in a row, and a defender who has to be right twice.



The idea to carry into lecture 3.6 is that these six screens are a parts list. The actions that carry names on a broadcast are built from two or three of them in sequence, run for a particular player, and the next lecture takes the most common of those apart into the parts you have just seen.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
text:
New terms introduced (10): Delay, Double drag, Drag screen, Dribble handoff, Early offense, Flow offense, Get action, Pistol, Trailer flip, Zoom. Diagrams: 7.
Lecture 3.1 ended with the defense back but back badly: five defenders in the front court, cross-matched, the big still arriving, nobody yet in the stance they will be in ten seconds from now. Early offense is the set of actions built for exactly that state. It is not the break, because the numbers are even. It is not the half court, because the defense is not set. It is the ten seconds in between, and a team that has a plan for those ten seconds gets a good shot before the other team has finished getting organized.
Two things make the window worth attacking. First, the defense has matched up by proximity, not by assignment, so a guard may be standing next to a big and a big next to a guard. Second, the last defender back is usually the big, and the last attacker up is usually the other big. That trailing big is the whole subject of this lecture: he is the one player the defense has not accounted for, and every action below is a way of using him before they do.
This lecture takes the actions in the order a team learns them. Section 1 is the drag screen and the double drag, the trailing big screening the ball. Section 2 is pistol, the guard-to-wing entry. Section 3 is delay and the dribble handoff, the big holding the ball at the top of an empty floor. Section 4 is zoom and get action, the two handoff actions that start from a screen or a pass. Section 5 is what joins them: the trailer flip and flow, the rules that let a team run from one action into the next without a call. Each action is a card with the same five slots, and each card’s last slot names the coverage in Chapter 4 built to stop it.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 1 The trailing big screens the ball
text:
1 The trailing big screens the ball
The drag screen is a ball screen set on the run. The ball-handler is dribbling up one side of the floor; the big is trailing him; instead of running to the block the big runs at the ball-handler’s defender and sets a screen while that defender is still retreating. The screen is set before the defense has decided how to guard screens on this possession, which is the point. See Figure 1.






Figure 1: The drag screen. The trailing big arrives from behind and screens the ball-handler’s defender before his own defender has caught up. The handler comes off toward the middle; the big rolls into an empty lane.









Setup


The ball-handler on one side of the floor, above the arc, dribbling toward the front court with the defense matched but not set. The big trailing the ball by a few steps. The other three attackers filling the corners and the weak-side wing so the lane is empty.


Trigger


The big reaches the ball-handler’s defender before his own defender reaches him.


Read


The ball-handler comes off the screen toward the middle and reads the big’s defender. If that defender is late, the handler turns the corner and drives. If he has arrived and dropped back, the handler has a pull-up, and the big rolls. If he has arrived and stepped up to the ball, the pass to the rolling big is open behind him.


Payoff


A two-on-one against the big’s defender before the help defenders have found their assignments, so the roll or the pop is uncontested.


Beaten by


The big’s defender sprinting rather than jogging back, so he is level with the screen when it is set and can play it as a set defense would. Chapter 4 teaches the coverages; the one built for the drag is to ice it toward the sideline, taught in lecture 4.3, which also covers the drag in lecture 4.2.





Action 1: The drag screen: a ball screen set before the defense has decided how to guard one.



The double drag adds the second big. Two screeners line up one behind the other on the same side, and the ball-handler comes off both. The two screens do two different things: the first screener usually steps out to the arc for a pop, the second rolls to the rim. The defense now has three attackers in the action and only the two screeners’ defenders and the ball defender to handle them, which is what Figure 2 shows.






Figure 2: The double drag. Two trailing bigs screen in a staggered line. The handler comes off both; the first screener pops, the second rolls.









Setup


As the drag, with both bigs trailing on the same side and the two shooters in the corners.


Trigger


The first screener sets his screen; the second screener sets his a step later and a step further along the handler’s path.


Read


The handler comes off both screens toward the middle. The first big pops; the second rolls. The handler reads the second big’s defender: if he stays with the roller, the pop is open; if he steps up to stop the ball, the roll is open; if he splits the difference, the handler shoots.


Payoff


Two bigs in two different places, one at the arc and one at the rim, guarded by defenders who arrived at different times and have not talked.


Beaten by


The two screeners’ defenders sorting out before the screens who will take the pop and who will take the roll, which is the same discipline as any pick-and-roll coverage in lecture 4.3, done on the run.





Action 2: The double drag: one screen becomes two, and one read becomes three.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 2 Pistol: pass ahead, follow the pass
text:
2 Pistol: pass ahead, follow the pass
Pistol starts with a pass rather than a dribble. The point guard, bringing the ball up one side, throws ahead to the wing and then sprints toward the wing himself. The wing dribbles at him and hands the ball back, so the guard receives it moving toward the middle with the wing’s body between him and his defender. The big trails to the top of the key, and the second part of pistol is a ball screen from that big on whichever side the handoff has opened. It is called 21 because the 2 and the 1 run it. See Figure 3.






Figure 3: Pistol. The guard passes ahead to the wing and follows the pass; the wing hands the ball back so the guard receives it moving toward the middle. The big trails at the top for the screen that follows.









Setup


The point guard above the arc on one side, the wing ahead of him at the free-throw line extended, the big trailing to the top, the other two spaced on the weak side.


Trigger


The pass ahead. The guard’s defender relaxes for one step because his man no longer has the ball.


Read


The guard follows the pass. If his defender goes under the handoff, the guard keeps the ball and shoots or turns down toward the trailing big’s screen. If his defender chases over the top, the guard takes the handoff and drives the middle. If the wing’s defender jumps to the guard, the wing keeps the ball and drives baseline, which is the fake handoff.


Payoff


The best ball-handler receives the ball at speed, going toward the middle, with a screen already coming from the trailing big.


Beaten by


Switching the handoff, so the wing’s defender takes the guard and the guard’s defender stays with the wing. Switching is lecture 4.5; the specific answer to a handoff, which is to switch it or to top-lock the receiver so he cannot get to it, is in lecture 4.2.





Action 3: Pistol: the guard gives the ball up to get it back moving.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 3 Delay: the big at the top of an empty floor
text:
3 Delay: the big at the top of an empty floor
Delay gives the ball to the big instead of the guard. The center walks the ball to the top of the key and holds it, and the other four spread to the wings and corners: a 5-out floor with nobody in the paint, taught in lecture 3.10. From there the big has three things he can do, and the defense has to be ready for all three: hand the ball to a guard cutting up to him, screen for a guard who cuts past him without the ball, or reverse the ball to the other side. The most common is the handoff, and Figure 4 shows it.






Figure 4: Delay. The center holds the ball at the top of a 5-out floor. A guard cuts up from the wing to take a handoff; the far corner lifts to keep the spacing. The paint is empty because every defender is guarding a player outside the arc.









Setup


The center at the top with the ball. Two wings, two corners. Every defender is outside the paint because every attacker is.


Trigger


The big’s defender steps back to protect the rim, because that is where he wants to be, and leaves the big alone with the ball at the arc.


Read


One guard cuts up toward the big. The big reads the cutter’s defender. If the defender trails the cutter, the big hands the ball off and the guard drives downhill off his body. If the defender goes under, the big keeps the ball and the guard fades to the arc for a pass. If the defender jumps the handoff early, the big drives himself, into a paint nobody is protecting.


Payoff


A handoff with the whole paint empty behind it, so the driver meets one defender at most.


Beaten by


The big’s defender refusing to drop, guarding the big at the arc and denying the handoff, which puts a rim protector twenty-five feet from the rim; or switching every handoff. Both are in lecture 4.2.





Action 4: Delay: the big holds the ball where his defender does not want to guard him.



The dribble handoff deserves its own card, because it is the unit every action in this lecture is built from. A handoff is a pass and a screen in one motion: the player with the ball dribbles at a teammate, the teammate takes the ball out of his hands, and the first player’s body is in the way of the second player’s defender. It is legal because the handoff is not a screen under the rules; the handler is allowed to stand where he stopped. See Figure 5.






Figure 5: The dribble handoff. The big dribbles from the elbow toward the wing; the guard steps up and takes the ball as they pass. The big’s body screens the guard’s trailing defender, and the guard receives the ball already moving downhill.









Setup


One player with the ball and a live dribble, a teammate within a few steps, the teammate’s defender trailing him or level with him.


Trigger


The handler dribbles at the teammate, and the teammate steps toward the handler so the exchange happens at speed.


Read


The receiver reads his own defender. Trailing: take the handoff and drive off the handler’s hip. Under: refuse the handoff, or take it and shoot, because the defender has gone the long way round. Jumping the handoff: the handler keeps the ball and drives, because the defender has left his man to guard the exchange.


Payoff


The receiver gets the ball with a defender behind him rather than in front of him, which is the same thing a ball screen buys, without a screen the defense can call out.


Beaten by


Switching the exchange, so the receiver’s new defender is already in front of him; or the receiver’s defender going under and the receiver not being a shooter. See lecture 4.2.





Action 5: The dribble handoff: a pass and a screen in one motion, and the unit everything else here is built from.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 4 Zoom and get: the handoff that starts somewhere else
text:
4 Zoom and get: the handoff that starts somewhere else
Zoom puts a screen before the handoff. A shooter starts in the corner; a big sets a pin-down on the shooter’s defender; the shooter runs up off the screen toward the wing; and the ball-handler, who has been dribbling toward the same spot, hands him the ball as he arrives. The shooter has now used two screens in a row, the pin-down and the handler’s body, and is going downhill at full speed while his defender has been hit twice. It is also called Chicago action. The two frames of Figure 6 and Figure 7 show the screen and then the handoff.






Figure 6: Zoom, first frame. The shooter starts in the corner. The big pins down on his defender and he runs up toward the wing; the ball-handler dribbles toward the same spot.









Figure 7: Zoom, second frame. The shooter takes the handoff at the wing at full speed and turns the corner. The pin-down screener has rolled into the lane and the handler has stepped out to the arc.









Setup


The shooter in the corner, a big on the block above him ready to screen, the ball-handler above the arc on the same side, the other two spaced on the weak side.


Trigger


The pin-down. The shooter’s defender is hit by the screen and is now a step behind.


Read


The shooter comes off the pin-down and reads his defender while the handler dribbles at him. Trailing: take the handoff and drive. Going under the pin-down: curl the screen straight to the rim, and the handler passes instead of handing off. Switched, so the big’s defender has jumped out to the shooter: the big who screened rolls into the lane against a smaller defender.


Payoff


A shooter with a live dribble going downhill with his defender two screens behind, or a big rolling against a switched guard.


Beaten by


Top-locking the shooter before the pin-down so he cannot get to the handoff, taught in lecture 4.4, or switching the pin-down and living with the big on the guard.





Action 6: Zoom: a pin-down that flows into a handoff, so the receiver is already moving when he gets the ball.



Get action is the handoff started by a pass. The guard passes to the big at the elbow and follows his pass straight at him. The big turns and hands the ball back as the guard goes by. It is the give and go of lecture 3.7 with a handoff instead of a return pass, and it starts a possession in two seconds from a standstill, which is why teams run it out of a dead ball as often as out of the break. See Figure 8.






Figure 8: Get action. The guard passes to the big at the elbow and runs straight at him; the big hands the ball back as the guard passes and the guard drives off his body.









Setup


The guard with the ball above the arc, the big at the elbow or the slot on the same side, the other three spaced away.


Trigger


The pass to the big. The guard’s defender takes one step off his man, because the man does not have the ball.


Read


The guard runs at the big. Same three reads as the handoff: trailing, take it and drive; under, refuse or shoot; the big’s defender jumping the handoff, the big keeps it and drives.


Payoff


The guard has the ball back, moving, off a big’s body, two seconds after the possession started.


Beaten by


The guard’s defender staying attached through the pass, which denies the handoff and leaves the big with the ball at the elbow, a poor place for most bigs; or the switch. See lecture 4.2.





Action 7: Get action: the give and go with a handoff in place of the return pass.

title: 3.2: Early Offense
section: 5 Flow: how one action becomes the next
text:
5 Flow: how one action becomes the next
None of these actions is meant to be run once and stopped. The trailer flip is the hinge between the break and the half court: the trailing big arrives at the top, takes the reversal pass from the side the ball came up, and swings it to the other side in one motion. Where the drag screen uses the trailing big as a screener, the flip uses him as a passer, and a team usually has a rule for which one he does: screen if the ball is on his side, flip if it is not.
Flow is the name for offense that runs from transition into these actions and then into the half court without a play being called. It is governed by rules rather than a script. The rules are simple and a team’s are its own: which big trails and which rim runs; whether the trailer screens or flips; who fills the corners; what the wing does when the ball comes to him with a big trailing (in most systems, the pistol handoff). What flow buys is time. A called play takes three or four seconds to set up, and in those seconds the defense finishes getting organized. Flow spends those seconds attacking instead.
The idea to carry into lecture 3.3 is that every action here is a version of one thing: getting the ball to a player who is moving, past a defender who is not yet where he wants to be. The half-court offense in the lectures that follow has to manufacture that against a defense that is set, and its main tool for doing so is the ball screen, which the drag has already introduced.

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
New terms introduced (4): Isolation, Mismatch, Motion offense, Read and react. Diagrams: 4.
Nine lectures have named actions. This one is about the offenses that do not call them. A set play tells five players what to do; a conceptual offense tells them what to do if. The instructions are rules attached to events: if the ball is passed, screen away; if a teammate drives at you, cut behind him; if you are denied, back cut. Nobody calls anything, and the actions of lectures 3.2 to 3.9 appear anyway, because the rules produce them.
Section 1 is motion offense, the oldest of these. Section 2 is read and react, the most systematic. Section 3 is the two situations in which an offense deliberately stops moving: isolation and the mismatch. Section 4 is the synthesis this chapter has been building toward: every “beaten by” slot in Chapter 3 is a coverage from Chapter 4, and choosing the action that beats the coverage being shown is what an offense actually does.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
1 Motion offense
Motion offense gives each player a small set of rules about what to do when the ball moves. The classic pair is pass and screen away and fill the spot behind, as in Figure 1. The ball goes from the slot to the wing; the passer screens for someone on the far side rather than cutting toward the ball; the man he screens comes up to fill the spot the passer left. The floor is back in its shape, the ball is on a new side, and the rules apply again.






Figure 1: Motion offense. The ball is passed to the wing; the passer screens away for the far slot; that player fills the spot the passer left. No play was called: each player is following a rule about what to do when the ball moves.









Setup


Four or five players around the perimeter in named spots, one big inside or all five out, and a rule set every player knows.


Trigger


Any pass. The rules are attached to the ball moving.


Read


The passer chooses between the rules his team allows: screen away, cut through, or hold. The screened player reads his own defender with the four reads of lecture 3.5. Every other player fills so the spacing of lecture 3.10 is preserved. If the defense switches everything, the rules produce a mismatch and the offense stops and plays Section 3.


Payoff


Continuous screening and cutting that a defense must guard correctly every time, from an offense that can be run at any tempo and needs no call.


Beaten by


Switching everything, which turns every screen into a non-event and dares the offense to beat a matched-up defense one-on-one; or physical denial that stops the first pass. Lecture 4.5.





Action 1: Motion offense: rules attached to the pass, and the actions appear on their own.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
2 Read and react
Read and react attaches the rules to the drive rather than the pass, and it is the most explicit version of a conceptual offense: each player has a specified reaction to each thing the ball does, learned in layers, as in Figure 2. A baseline drive makes the man behind it circle to the spot it left, the weak-side corner lift to the wing, and the players away from the ball move up a spot. A drive at a teammate makes him cut behind it, which is the 45 cut of lecture 3.7. A pass to the post makes the passer and the nearest teammate cut in opposite directions.






Figure 2: Read and react. The drive is the signal. The player behind the drive fills the spot it left, the weak-side corner lifts, and the man at the top fills behind. Each reaction is a rule triggered by the direction of the drive.









Setup


4-out or 5-out spacing with every player in a named spot, and a rule for each of: a drive at you, a drive away from you, a pass to the post, a dribble at you.


Trigger


A drive, a dribble-at, or a post entry. Not a call.


Read


The driver reads the help exactly as in lecture 3.10. Everyone else executes their reaction without waiting to see whether the drive succeeds, which is what makes the passes available at the instant the help commits.


Payoff


Every drive has three outlets already moving to the right places before the help has finished committing.


Beaten by


A defense that never helps, so no reaction is ever triggered, which requires five defenders who can guard the ball alone; or shrinking the floor so the drives are into single gaps. Lecture 4.4.





Action 2: Read and react: the drive is the signal, and everyone else has a rule for it.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
text:
3 When the offense stops moving
Two situations are worth stopping for.
Isolation clears one side of the floor so one attacker can work alone, as in Figure 3. Everything this chapter has built exists to make two defenders guard one attacker; an isolation is the admission that this particular attacker beats one defender by himself, and the four teammates are there only to keep their own defenders too far away to help. It is the least collective thing an offense does, and it is correct whenever the individual advantage is larger than the advantage a screen would create.






Figure 3: Isolation. The other four attackers have cleared to the far side; the handler has the whole side of the floor and his defender has no help nearer than the nail.









Setup


The handler on a wing or at the top. The other four on the opposite side, spread so their defenders cannot help without leaving a shooter.


Trigger


A favorable individual matchup, or a late shot clock, or an ATO designed for it.


Read


The handler reads whether help comes. No help: beat the man. Help from the nail: the pass back to the top. Help from the weak-side corner: the skip. A second defender arriving on the dribble: the isolation has become a two-on-one and the read is the same as the drive’s.


Payoff


A one-on-one against the defender the offense chose, with no help within a pass.


Beaten by


A defender who stays in front, which is the whole answer; or a defense that sends a second defender early and lives with the pass out. Lecture 4.4.





Action 3: Isolation: clear the side and let one player beat one player.



A mismatch is the same idea created by the defense rather than chosen by the offense. After a switch, a big is guarding a guard or a guard is guarding a big, as in Figure 4. Both are attackable and each has its own route: the guard drives the slower defender, or the big posts the smaller one, which is the post-up and the early seal of lecture 3.7. The defense’s answer is the scram switch of lecture 4.5, which is why the early seal has to be early.






Figure 4: The mismatch. A switch has left a big on the guard and a guard on the big. Two ways to attack it: drive the slower defender, or post the smaller one.









Setup


A switch has just happened. The three players not involved space away to keep help out of the picture.


Trigger


The switch itself. The window is a second or two before the defense fixes it.


Read


Which mismatch is bigger. A guard against a slow big: attack off the dribble before help arrives. A big against a small guard: seal and call for the ball immediately, because a scram switch is coming. If the defense sends help, the man the helper left is open.


Payoff


A drive or a post catch against a defender who cannot guard that player alone.


Beaten by


The scram switch, or switching back at the first dead ball, or a defense whose players are similar enough in size that no switch creates a mismatch at all. Lecture 4.5.





Action 4: The mismatch: the defense made it; take whichever half is bigger, quickly.
crumbs: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters

title: 3.11: Motion, Conceptual Offense, Reads and Counters
section: 4 The synthesis: read the coverage, pick the action
text:
4 The synthesis: read the coverage, pick the action
Every card in this chapter ends with a “beaten by” slot, and every one of those slots names a coverage from Chapter 4. Reading them the other way round gives the offense’s actual decision procedure, because a coverage that beats one action is usually what makes another one available:

The defense drops on ball screens, conceding the pull-up to protect the rim. Then the pop and the pull-up are open, and the snake gets to them.
The defense plays at the level or hedges, killing the pull-up. Then the slip and the ghost punish the early commitment, and the rocket pass beats the hedge.
The defense traps, taking the ball out of the best player’s hands. Then the short roll and the 4-on-3 are the whole answer.
The defense ices toward the sideline. Then the step-up screen sends the handler baseline instead, and the twist re-screens him back to the middle.
The defense switches everything. Then screens stop mattering and mismatch, early seal and isolation are what is left, which is why switching teams need five players who can guard.
The defense top-locks shooters off screens. Then the back cut is open behind the lock, every time.
The defense helps hard from the weak side. Then the hammer, the kick-out and the skip pass are the punishment.
The defense never helps. Then the drive and the isolation are the offense, because nobody is guarding two players.

This is what a good offense is doing while it looks like it is running a play: showing an action, seeing the coverage, and running the action that beats it. The named actions of lectures 3.4 and 3.6 exist for exactly this reason, which is why each of them was introduced with the coverage it was invented against.
The idea to carry into lecture 3.12 is that all of this assumes a live ball and a set defense. The next lecture is about the possessions that start from neither: out of bounds, after a timeout, against a press, and against a zone.

title: 2.1: What Is Different Now
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
Chapter 1 gave dates. This chapter gives measurements, and it is the chapter where this site is most likely to be wrong, because a number is easy to state and hard to check. So every figure below comes from one saved table of league averages, every figure names the season it belongs to, and where a claim is commonly made that this site cannot check, it appears as a gap rather than as a sentence.
One methodological note first, because it changes how the rest of this lecture reads. The table these numbers come from carries two sets of league averages on one page, regular season and playoffs, with the same column names and the same season labels.1 The playoff rows look exactly like the regular-season rows and are different numbers. Everything below is regular season, and the saved extraction labels every row with the table it came from, so that a reader can check which is which.

Three things in that table are worth saying plainly.
The line’s first season barely used it. In 1979-80, the season the three-point shot was adopted, teams attempted 2.8 of them a game out of 90.6 shots.2 That is the rule existing and nobody using it, which is the subject of lecture 1.4.
The rate did not rise steadily. It was higher in 1996-97 than in 2004-05. A reader told only that “three-point shooting has increased since the line was introduced” would predict a smooth climb and be wrong about two decades of it.
The change since 2004-05 is the large one. From 19.7% of shots to 42.2% is the shift that produced the offense of Chapter 3: the spacing, the corner three, the kick-out, the 5-out floor.

Why this lecture opens at 2004-05. The plan for this site anchors Chapter 2 at the 2004-05 rule cluster, on the same criterion Chapter 1 uses: a boundary is a dated rule change. The rule usually named for that season is the elimination of hand-checking, and this site has no source on file for it: NBA.com’s own season review of 2004-05 does not mention a rule change.3 So 2004-05 is used here as the season the measurements pivot around, which the table shows, and not as a rule change, which this site cannot yet source.

What has changed more than pace is what a possession is worth. title: 2.1: What Is Different Now
text:
3 Efficiency and free throws
True shooting percentage is one number that accounts for twos, threes and free throws together. It was .531 in 1979-80, .529 in 2004-05, and .576 in 2024-25.6 Two decades of essentially no change, then a substantial rise.
Free throws moved the other way. Attempts per game were 27.8 in 1979-80, 26.1 in 2004-05, 22.8 in 2014-15 and 21.7 in 2024-25.7 The modern game scores more while shooting fewer free throws, which is worth holding against the common assumption that the increase in scoring is an increase in fouls called.

4 What this lecture does not claim

Shot location is not sourced here. The claim that the mid-range shot has largely disappeared, and that shots have moved to the rim and the arc, is true as far as this site’s authors know and is not on file. The source that publishes shot-location data as a public table is Cleaning the Glass, and its team pages returned HTTP 500 when this site tried to acquire them on 2026-09-21; the league’s own stats pages render their tables with script, and the acquisition tool saved 443 words of page furniture and no data. What would close it: a shot-location table from a source that serves it as HTML, or a saved export.


Positionless lineups and small ball are not sourced here. Both are real and widely described, and neither is a measurement this site has. A count would need lineup data by position, which none of the sources on file carry. What would close it: a public table of lineup composition by season.

Those two gaps are worth as much as the numbers above them. A reader can take every figure in this lecture and check it against the saved table; the two claims in this section are the ones this site would be asking to be believed on, so it does not make them.
The idea to carry into lecture 2.2 is that the numbers here say what changed and not why. The next lecture is about the measurements that changed the decisions: points per possession, the value of a shot by location, and what it means for a shooter to have gravity.

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
A rule can exist for twenty years before anyone uses it properly. That is the story of this era: the three-point line arrived in 1979 and the sport spent two decades treating it as a specialty shot rather than as the thing an offense should be organized around. What the era is remembered for instead is two rookies, one dynasty, and the most physical defense the league has allowed.

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001
text:
1 The line nobody used
The rule that defines the era arrived complete and was ignored for most of it. What makes this striking is that the arithmetic was available from the first day: a shot worth three is worth taking at a lower success rate than a shot worth two, and the ratio is not subtle. The reason it took twenty years is not that anyone miscalculated but that nobody was counting, which is what lecture 2.2 is about.
The consequence for the vocabulary of this site is that most of Chapter 3 would have looked strange for most of this era. 5-out spacing, the corner three as a designed shot, the kick-out as the main assist: all of them presume the line is worth organizing around.
