3 The physical 1990s and Jordan
The back half of the era is the most physical defense the league has permitted, and the player who defined it is the one who had to play through it.






Player


Michael Jordan, guard, Chicago Bulls


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 5, in 1987-88, 1990-91, 1991-92, 1995-96 and 1997-98.10 Finals Most Valuable Player, 6, which is more rows than any other name on that list.11 Hall of Fame, Class of 2009.12


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The defining player of the era in which defenses were allowed to be at their most physical, and the reason several of the rules about them were rewritten after he stopped.





Player 3: Michael Jordan: six Finals MVP awards, the most on the league’s list.



The defensive rules of this era are the reason isolation was a primary offense rather than a late-clock option. A defense was not permitted to play what would now be called a zone: the illegal-defense rules required defenders to be guarding someone, which meant an attacker who cleared one side of the floor genuinely had it to himself. The isolation of lecture 3.11 is what an offense does when the rules guarantee no help arrives from the weak side.

title: 1.4: The Three-Point Line, 1979 to 2001
text:
4 What changed in 2001
The rules that ended the era did two things. They removed the prohibition on illegal defense, which permitted zone defenses in the professional game for the first time. And they introduced the defensive three-second rule, which prevented a defender from simply standing in the lane to take the rim away, by requiring him to be “actively guarding an opponent within three seconds.”13
Those two changes together produce the game Chapter 3 describes. A defense may now be anywhere, so long as nobody parks in the paint; an offense must therefore create space rather than be handed it; and spacing, the drive and the kick-out become the organizing ideas. That is the subject of lecture 1.5.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
Eight years separate the first professional season that lasted from the rule that made the professional game watchable. This is the shortest era in the chapter and the one with the clearest ending: the sport acquired a single league, discovered that a league can be won by not playing, and fixed it with a clock.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
1 One league
The BAA began in 1946-47 and was not alone: the National Basketball League already existed. The two merged, and NBA.com’s account of the 1949-50 season states the terms: “the summer of 1949 solidified the professional basketball picture, with the six surviving NBL teams being absorbed into the BAA and the league being renamed the National Basketball Association.”1
That single sentence contains the whole of what this era did structurally. The name the league has used ever since dates from that summer, and the season that followed was the first played under it.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
2 Mikan
The era’s defining player was George Mikan, whose Minneapolis Lakers won the first NBA season: NBA.com’s review of 1949-50 records the season “in which the Minneapolis Lakers emerged as NBA champions” and that “George Mikan led the league” that year.2 He was inducted into the Hall of Fame in its inaugural class, which the Hall’s own list records as “Class of 1959”,3 and Wikipedia’s account of that class adds that he “was the first NBA player to be enshrined.”4






Player


George Mikan, center, Minneapolis Lakers


Standing


Hall of Fame, Class of 1959, inducted as a player in the inaugural class.5 NBA championship, 1949-50, with Minneapolis.6


Second bearing


The induction is confirmed by a second publisher.7 The championship is on one publisher only.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The first player the league wrote rules about rather than for, and the reason the lane was widened while he was still playing.





Player 1: George Mikan: the first player whose presence changed the rules written around him.



The post-up of lecture 3.7 is the action this era was built on, and Mikan is the reason. An offense whose best player stands near the rim with his back to it is an offense that does not need spacing, a three-point line or a ball screen, and for most of this era it did not have any of them.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
section: 3 Bob Cousy and the first fast break
text:
3 Bob Cousy and the first fast break
The other player this lecture cards is the one who made the ball move. Bob Cousy won the Most Valuable Player award once, in 1956-57, which is the single row naming him on the league’s year-by-year list,8 and he entered the Hall of Fame in the Class of 1971.9






Player


Bob Cousy, point guard, Boston Celtics


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 1, in 1956-57.10 Hall of Fame, Class of 1971.11

Why he mattered


The first guard whose passing was the reason a team ran, and the player the early transition game was built around.





Player 2: Bob Cousy: the ball moving ahead of the defense, twenty years before anyone counted what that was worth.



His award falls just after this era’s boundary, which is worth stating rather than smoothing over: the MVP award did not exist during most of the founding league, and a player whose best years were before an award cannot be measured by it. That is the reason this chapter counts honors rather than compares them across eras.

title: 1.2: The Founding League, 1946 to 1954
text:
4 The clock
The era ends with an arithmetic problem. Nothing in the rules obliged a team with a lead to shoot, so the rational thing to do with a lead was to hold the ball, and teams did. NBA.com’s review of the 1954-55 season records the fix: “it was the adoption of the 24-second clock and an accompanying limit on the number of fouls a team could commit in a quarter.”12 The same page names its author, “Syracuse owner Danny Biasone and his GM, Leo Ferris, came up with the shot clock idea”,13 and quotes the former coach and referee Charlie Eckman: “Danny Biasone saved the NBA with the 24-second rule, make no mistake about that”.14
The clock is the most consequential rule in this chapter, because it created the thing every later lecture assumes: a possession with an end. Pace becomes a number only once possessions are countable, late clock becomes a situation only once there is a clock to be late on, and transition becomes worth measuring only once the alternative has a deadline.
The idea to carry into lecture 1.3 is that the clock did not make the game fast. It made it finite, and the twenty-five years that follow are the sport working out what to do with a possession that has to end.

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
Chapter 3 taught what a possession is made of and Chapter 4 will teach how it is stopped. This chapter is about where those things came from, and it is organized on one rule: an era begins and ends at a dated event, not at a change in how the basketball looked. A rule change is a date. A league merging with another is a date. “The game got faster in the sixties” is an impression, and impressions make boundaries that cannot be checked, so this chapter does not use them. Each era below is bounded by an event with a source, and where the date of an event is not on file, this site says so rather than guessing.
This lecture covers the first fifty-five years: one gymnasium, thirteen rules, and no professional league that lasted.

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
1 The invention
The game was invented on purpose, by one person, in response to a specific problem. Springfield College records that “the game was invented by Springfield College instructor and graduate student James Naismith in 1891”,1 and that the class it was invented for met in “the winter of 1891-1892”.2 Naismith had been given a class of restless students and a charge from Luther Gulick, the school’s physical education superintendent, to devise an indoor activity that would hold them.
What he produced was, in the college’s own account, an adaptation of several games then played: passing from American rugby, the jump ball from English rugby, the goal from lacrosse. He asked the janitor for two boxes and was given two peach baskets, which he nailed to the rail of the gymnasium’s running track. Then he “drew up the 13 original rules, which described, among other facets, the method of moving the ball and what constituted a foul.”3
Two things in that account matter for the rest of this site. The first is that the goal was horizontal and above the players’ heads, which is why nearly every action in Chapter 3 is about arriving at a spot rather than crossing a line. The second is that a foul was defined in the first thirteen rules, which is why the defensive vocabulary of Chapter 4 is so largely a vocabulary about what a defender may not do.

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
2 What the game looked like
For most of this era the game had two features that no modern viewer would recognize.
A center jump after every score. Possession was contested at the middle of the floor after each basket rather than handed to the conceding team, so a team with a dominant center could win possession repeatedly and a game could be a series of jump balls.
The set shot. The jump shot was not yet standard; the standard shot was taken with both feet on the floor. A game played with set shots from distance and a contested jump after every basket produced scores that look like misprints beside modern ones.
This is also the era in which the game spread furthest fastest, through the YMCA network and the colleges, and the reason it did is that the rules fitted on a page. Springfield College records that “a few weeks after the game was invented, students introduced the game at their own YMCAs.”4

title: 1.1: Origins, 1891 to 1946
text:
3 The professional game before 1946
Professional leagues existed in this period and did not last. The one that ends this era is the Basketball Association of America, which played its first season in 1946-47 and is described by the league itself as “the precursor to the modern-day NBA”.5 That season was sixty games long, and NBA.com’s own account of it notes that “television was still in the future, and radio broadcasts were hardly universal.”6

No star cards in this era. The awards this chapter counts (Most Valuable Player, Finals Most Valuable Player) did not exist before the 1950s, and the only reachable primary source for a figure from this period is the Hall of Fame’s own inductee list, which gives a class year and no playing record. Rather than describe players from memory, this site leaves the era without star cards and names the gap. James Naismith is on that list as a contributor, in the Class of 1959, and he appears here as the inventor rather than as a player.

The idea to carry into lecture 1.2 is that the game had spread across a continent before anyone had built a professional league capable of surviving a decade. The next lecture is about the league that did, and about what it had to change to hold an audience.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
The longest era in this chapter, and the one that most resembles the game as a set of principles rather than as a set of shots. Every possession now had a deadline; nothing yet rewarded shooting from distance. What the sport did with those twenty-five years is work out how to score near the rim against a defense that knew you had to.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
section: 1 What a possession without a three-point line is
text:
1 What a possession without a three-point line is
A modern viewer reading Chapter 3 might assume spacing is a permanent feature of basketball. It is not; it is a consequence of the three-point line, and this era is the proof. If every shot is worth two points, a shot from twenty-three feet is a worse version of a shot from ten, and there is no reason for an attacker to stand beyond the arc except to make room. Gap as a measurement means little when no defender is obliged to guard a man twenty-five feet from the rim.
So the offense of this era crowds the paint on purpose, the post-up is the central action, and the defense is built to stop shots close to the basket. The cross screen of lecture 3.5 and the high-low of lecture 3.7 are this era’s characteristic actions, and both exist to get one big man the ball on the block against another.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
2 Russell and Chamberlain
The era’s two defining players played the same position in opposite ways, and the league’s own year-by-year award lists record the result.






Player


Bill Russell, center, Boston Celtics


Standing

The two inductions are confirmed as two by a second publisher.3


Why he mattered


The player who made defense the thing a team could be built on, in the era when the shot clock had just made every possession finite.





Player 1: Bill Russell: five MVP awards, and a second Hall of Fame induction forty-six years after the first.

Why he mattered


The other half of the era’s defining argument, and the player whose dominance produced more rule changes than any other.





Player 2: Wilt Chamberlain: four MVP awards, and one Finals MVP, because the award began in 1969.



The Finals MVP entry is worth pausing on, because it is a case where a count means less than it looks. NBA.com’s page states that “since 1969, the NBA has honored the NBA Finals’ best performer”,7 so a player whose best seasons were in the early 1960s could not have won it however he played. This is the clearest reason this chapter counts honors within an era rather than comparing totals across eras: the things being counted did not exist for the same length of time.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
section: 3 Abdul-Jabbar, and why a career is not an era
text:
3 Abdul-Jabbar, and why a career is not an era
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar’s six Most Valuable Player awards are the most on the league’s list, and they fall on both sides of this era’s ending: three with Milwaukee in the early 1970s and three with the Lakers, the last of them in 1979-80, the first season of the next era.8






Player


Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, center, Milwaukee Bucks, Los Angeles Lakers


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 6, in 1970-71, 1971-72, 1973-74, 1975-76, 1976-77 and 1979-80, which is more than any other name on the league’s list.9 Finals Most Valuable Player, 2, in 1970-71 and 1984-85.10 Hall of Fame, Class of 1995.11


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


A career that spans two of this chapter’s eras, which is the clearest evidence that an era boundary is a rule change rather than a change of personnel.





Player 3: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar: six MVP awards across two eras, and fourteen years between his two Finals MVPs.



That span is the argument for how this chapter is organized. If eras were defined by who was playing, Abdul-Jabbar’s career would be one era, and it would include both the game before the three-point line and the game after it. Because eras here are defined by dated rule changes, his career crosses a boundary, which is what a career is supposed to do.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
4 The ABA and the merger
The rival American Basketball Association operated through the back half of this era and ended in 1976, when several of its teams joined the NBA. Its lasting contribution is the line that ends this lecture: the three-point shot was an ABA feature before it was an NBA one.

The merger is not sourced here. This site has NBA.com’s season recaps for the boundary seasons on file, and none of them states the 1976 merger or its terms. The claim above about the ABA and the three-point line rests on the 1979-80 recap, which says the shot was “a popular facet of the ABA game”;12 the merger itself is stated here without a source on file, and will carry one or be removed when the sourcing pass for this chapter reaches it.

title: 1.3: The Shot-Clock Game, 1954 to 1979
text:
5 The line
The era ends with a rule adopted from the competitor that had just folded into it. NBA.com’s review of 1979-80 records it plainly: “the 3-point field goal, a popular facet of the ABA game, was adopted by the league.”13 The same page notes what everyone remembers about that season instead: it “would forever be known as the year Larry Bird and Earvin” Magic Johnson arrived.14
Both things are true, and the ordering is the point of this chapter. The rookies are what the season is remembered for; the line is what changed the sport.

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
text:
No new terms introduced. No diagrams.
This is the era the rest of this site is written about. Every action in Chapter 3 and every coverage in Chapter 4 is the current game, and the current game begins when the rules stopped guaranteeing an attacker one-on-one space and stopped allowing a defender to stand in the lane. What happened afterwards is that the sport spent twenty years discovering that the answer to both was spacing.

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
section: 1 What the two rule changes did to the floor
text:
1 What the two rule changes did to the floor
Removing illegal defense allowed a defense to be anywhere. Defensive three seconds stopped it being in the lane, because a defender there must be “actively guarding an opponent within three seconds.”1 Together they replace one arrangement of the floor with another.
Under the old rules, an offense that cleared a side got a genuine one-on-one, because the defense was forbidden to zone up behind it. Under the new ones it does not, because help may come from anywhere; but help also cannot sit and wait at the rim. So the offense’s problem changes from “beat your man with no help coming” to “make the help come from somewhere it cannot afford to leave”. That is the whole of lecture 3.10: the gap, the drive, the kick-out, the skip pass.
Three consequences follow, and each is an entire lecture elsewhere on this site.
The pick-and-roll becomes the main action. A ball screen is the cheapest way to make two defenders guard one attacker, and the rules now permit the defense a dozen answers, which is why lecture 4.3 has six coverages in it and lecture 3.4 has five actions invented to beat them.
Spacing becomes the organizing idea. 5-out and 4-out 1-in exist to keep help far away, and the corner three becomes the shot an offense is built to produce because it is the shot the help defender has to leave to guard.
The big man’s job changes. The center of lecture 3.10 is a screener, a roller and a rim protector; the post-up that was the whole offense in lecture 1.3 becomes one option among many, used mostly against a mismatch.

2 Nash and the Suns
The case for the current game was made publicly, and early, by one team.






Player


Steve Nash, point guard, Phoenix Suns


Standing


Most Valuable Player, 2, in 2004-05 and 2005-06.2 Hall of Fame, Class of 2018.3


Second bearing


Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)


Why he mattered


The player whose team made the case for pace and spacing in the first seasons after the paint opened, several years before the rest of the league agreed.





Player 1: Steve Nash: two MVP awards for playing the way the rules had just started to reward.



NBA.com’s review of the first of those seasons describes what it looked like at the time: “Nash set the league ablaze with a frenetic pace that resulted in a league-best 62 regular-season wins for the Phoenix Suns and an MVP award for Nash.”4 The word the page reaches for is pace, which is the measurement lecture 2.1 takes up.

3 Duncan, and the era’s overlap
The other player carded here won the league’s highest individual award in the first two seasons after the rule change, playing the position the change was supposed to have devalued.






Player


Tim Duncan, forward, San Antonio Spurs


Standing

Each is on one publisher.(single publisher)

The last player to win the league’s highest individual honor as a traditional big man on both sides of the rule change that opened the paint.





Player 2: Tim Duncan: MVP in the first two seasons of the new rules, and Finals MVP in the last season of the old ones.



His Finals MVP rows straddle the boundary: one in 1998-99, under the old rules, and two afterwards.8 That is worth stating because it is the honest version of what a rule change does. It does not end careers or reverse who is good. It changes what a team has to do to get a shot, and the players who were already good at the new thing get better.

title: 1.5: The Paint Opens, 2001 to the Present
text:
4 The take foul, 2022-23
One later rule change is on file with a primary source, and it is the one lecture 4.1 is built around. The league announced in July 2022 that “beginning with the 2022-23 NBA season” the penalty for a transition take foul would be that “the offensive team will be awarded one free throw, which may be attempted by any player on the offensive team in the game at the time that the foul is committed.” and “the offensive team will retain possession of the ball.”9
It is a small rule with a clean mechanism: it made a tactic uneconomic rather than illegal. The team that fouls to stop a break now gives up a free throw and the ball, so the trade that made the foul worth it no longer works. That is the shape most modern rule changes take, and it is why this chapter’s boundaries are rule changes rather than trends: a rule changes the arithmetic on a specific day.

Hand-checking is not sourced here. The elimination of hand-checking is usually dated to 2004-05 and is usually named as a cause of the era’s scoring increase. NBA.com’s season review of 2004-05 is on file and does not mention it.10 So this lecture does not assert it. What would close the gap: the league’s own announcement of the rule change, or a rulebook edition carrying its adoption date.

Chapter 2 is about measurements: how much the three-point rate actually changed, what pace is now, where shots come from, and which of those claims this site can source and which it cannot. Chapters 3 and 4 are the game this era produced, action by action and coverage by coverage.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
New terms introduced (2): Corner three, Gravity. No diagrams.
Lecture 2.1 measured what changed. This lecture is about the measurement that caused it, and it is short, because the idea at its center is one division.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
1 Points per possession
Points per possession is points scored divided by possessions used. It is the currency of every argument in this site: a possession is the unit a team gets a fixed number of, so the only question about any action is how many points it returns per possession spent.
The reason this is the right unit and points per game is not is in the pace table of lecture 2.1. A team that plays fast scores more points per game without being better at scoring, and a team that plays slowly scores fewer without being worse. Dividing by possessions removes tempo from the comparison, which is what makes a 1979-80 offense and a 2024-25 offense comparable at all.
The figure this site already quotes for transition, in lecture 3.1, is of exactly this kind: a data set of play-by-play since the 2010 season gives “the average points per transition play is 1.04” against “the average points per half-court play is 0.87”.1 That is a difference of 0.17 points per play, and everything in lecture 3.1 is a way of getting more plays into the first category.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
2 The arithmetic of the three
The whole of the shift measured in lecture 2.1 follows from one comparison, and it needs no data beyond the values of the shots.
A two-point shot made at rate p returns 2p points. A three-point shot made at rate q returns 3q. The three is the better shot whenever 3q > 2p, which is whenever q > (2/3)p. So a three taken at 35% returns 1.05 points, and a two must be made at better than 52.5% to match it.
That is the entire argument, and it was available on the day the line was adopted in 1979. What was missing for twenty years was not the arithmetic but the habit of counting. Lecture 2.1 shows the consequence: threes went from 3.1% of shots in 1979-80 to 42.2% in 2024-25, and true shooting rose from .531 to .576 over the same span.2

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
3 The corner three
The corner three is where that arithmetic is sharpest, and the reason is geometry rather than skill. The three-point line is a fixed arc around the basket with the corner segments cut off by the sidelines. The NBA rulebook states it in one sentence: “The three-point field goal area has parallel lines 3’ from the sidelines, extending from the baseline and an arc of 23’9” from the middle of the basket which intersects the parallel lines.”3 A shot from the corner is therefore taken from 22 feet rather than 23 feet 9 inches, the shortest three available, and worth the same three points.
That single fact is why the corner is a place in this site’s vocabulary rather than merely a region of the floor. The lift of lecture 3.7 exists to get a shooter out of it and back to the wing when the drive goes baseline; the kick-out and skip pass of lecture 3.10 exist to find him in it; the hammer of lecture 3.6 exists to put a shooter there against the grain of a defense’s rotation.

The corner three’s higher conversion rate is not sourced here. It is routinely reported that corner threes are made at a higher rate than threes from above the break, which is what the shorter distance would predict. This site has no shot-location table on file, for the reasons stated in lecture 2.1, so the claim appears here as the geometry (which is in the rulebook) and not as a conversion rate (which is not on file). What would close it: a public shot-location table by zone.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
text:
4 Gravity
Gravity is the name for what a shooter does to defenders when he is not involved in the play. A defender who will not leave a shooter is a defender who is not helping, so the shooter’s presence is worth points scored by somebody else. It is the clearest case in this site of a term that exists because of a measurement: the idea that a player’s value can be located in shots he does not take requires someone to have counted what happens when he stands still.
Gravity is also why spacing is a property of a team rather than of a floor plan. Five players spread to the arc create nothing if their defenders can safely leave them; the same five spots occupied by shooters force every helper to make a choice. That is the difference between the 5-out alignment and 5-out as an offense.

Gravity is not quantified here. Several public and private analyses have put numbers on it. None of them is on file, so this lecture defines the term and does not measure it.

title: 2.2: The Analytics That Drove It
section: 5 How much of the modern game is downstream of one division
text:
5 How much of the modern game is downstream of one division
A reader can draw a line from 3q > 2p through most of Chapter 3.

The floor. 5-out and 4-out 1-in exist to place shooters where help must come from.
The gap. Spacing is measured in gaps because a double gap is the distance a helper cannot cover in time, and it only matters if leaving the man costs three points rather than two.
The main action. The pick-and-roll of lecture 3.3 forces two defenders onto one attacker, and the pop exists because the screener’s defender now has to choose between the rim and the arc.
The shot chart. The corner three became a designed shot, and the drive and kick-out became the pair of actions that produce it.

What does not follow from it is anything in Chapter 1. The eras there are bounded by dated rule changes, and the arithmetic in this lecture was true in every one of them. That is the honest summary of this chapter: the sport did not learn a new fact in 2004, it started acting on an old one, and the measurements in lecture 2.1 are the record of it doing so.

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
text:
New terms introduced (12): 45 cut, Back cut, Early seal, Flash, Give and go, High-low, Iverson cut, Lift, Pinch post, Post-up, Stampede cut, UCLA cut. Diagrams: 10.
Two lectures of screens have made it look as if a player without the ball gets open only when a teammate stands in someone’s way. Most of the time he does not have a screen. He has his defender’s eyes, his defender’s feet, and his own body, and the actions in this lecture are what he does with those three things. A cut is a change of direction timed to the moment a defender is looking somewhere else. A seal is a body placed between a defender and the spot the ball is going. Both are older than any screen, and every offense that runs without a script, which is lecture 3.11, is built on players who know them.
Section 1 is the post-up and the early seal, the two seals. Section 2 is the cuts that punish a defender’s eyes: the 45 cut, the back cut, the flash and the stampede. Section 3 is the two cuts that use a teammate’s body without a screen being called: the UCLA cut and the Iverson cut. Section 4 is the two-man passing actions: give and go and high-low. Section 5 is the lift and the pinch post, which are not cuts to score but movements that keep the floor spaced so the cuts work. Section 6 names the cuts heard for which there is no entry yet.

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
text:
1 The two seals
The post-up is the oldest way to get a shot near the rim. A player, usually a big, establishes position on the block with his back to the basket and his defender behind him, shows a target hand, and takes an entry pass, as in Figure 1. What he has bought is not a shot but a position: the ball a few feet from the rim, the defender on his back, and every move from there is a move the defender has to guess at. A post-up is also the standard way to use a mismatch: a bigger player against a smaller defender goes to the block, because that is where size matters most.






Figure 1: The post-up. The big holds position on the block with his back to the basket and his defender sealed behind him; the entry pass comes from the wing.









Setup


The big at the block, chest to the passer, wide stance, defender behind him. The passer on the wing, in the big’s line of sight. The other three spaced so no second defender is near the block.


Trigger


The big has the defender on his back and a hand up; the passer has a clear angle.


Read


The passer reads the defender’s position. Behind the big: the entry pass to the target hand. Playing on the high side, between the big and the ball: the big steps toward the baseline and the pass is a bounce pass to the low side. Fronting, between the big and the passer: the lob over the top, if the weak-side help is far enough away. After the catch, the big reads the help: one defender on him, a post move; a second defender coming, the kick-out to the shooter the help left.


Payoff


The ball a few feet from the rim, a defender who has to guess, and a double team that opens a shooter if it comes.


Beaten by


Fronting the post with weak-side help behind, so the lob is contested; or a dig from the nearest guard on the catch. Both in lecture 4.4.





Action 1: The post-up: position first, then the pass, then the read.



The early seal is the post-up done fast, against a switch. When a defense switches a screen, for an instant a small defender is guarding the big. The big does not roll or pop; he turns and pins the small defender under the rim before the defense can send help or switch back, and the pass comes over the top, as in Figure 2. The window is one or two seconds, which is why it is called early. The defense’s answer, the scram switch, is a defender rotating to take the big off the small man, and it is taught in lecture 4.5.






Figure 2: The early seal. A ball screen has just been switched; a guard-sized defender is on the big. The big pins him under the rim before help arrives and the pass goes over the top.









Setup


A ball screen against a switching defense. The big screening, the handler above him, the other three spaced wide so no help is near the lane.


Trigger


The switch: the big’s defender takes the ball and the handler’s smaller defender takes the big.


Read


The big turns into the small defender and drives him toward the rim with his hip and legs, arm up. The handler reads the help. None coming: the lob or the entry now. A defender rotating to the big: the shooter that defender left is open, and the pass goes there instead.


Payoff


A layup for the big against a guard, or an open shooter where the help came from.


Beaten by


The scram switch, in which a third defender takes the big and the small defender rotates out to the perimeter, before the entry pass; or a defense that switches only screens where the big cannot seal in time. Lecture 4.5.





Action 2: The early seal: the instant a switch puts a small defender on the big, pin him.

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
section: 2 Cuts that punish a defender’s eyes
text:
2 Cuts that punish a defender’s eyes
A defender guarding a player without the ball has two jobs at once: see his man, and see the ball. Every cut in this section is timed to the moment he chooses the ball.
The 45 cut is the cut made when a teammate drives. The wing player’s defender turns his head to the drive and takes a step toward the lane to help. The wing cuts to the rim behind him at a 45-degree angle, and the driver drops the ball off, as in Figure 3. It is the base cut of read-and-react offense, taught in lecture 3.11: the drive is the trigger and the cut is the rule.






Figure 3: The 45 cut. The ball is driven from the left. The right wing’s defender turns to the drive; the wing cuts to the rim at 45 degrees behind him for the drop-off.









Setup


A driver on one side. A wing player on the other, one pass away, with his defender between him and the ball.


Trigger


The defender’s head turns to the drive, or his feet move toward the lane.


Read


The wing cuts to the rim at 45 degrees, behind the defender. The driver reads: cutter open at the rim, drop it off; the defender recovers to the cutter, the spot the cutter left is empty and the next player fills it for a kick-out; the rim protector steps to the cutter, the driver has the layup.


Payoff


A layup off a drive that did not itself reach the rim, from a defender who looked at the ball.


Beaten by


Helping with the eyes and not the feet, so the defender stays with his man and the drive is left to the rim protector; or a stunt, a fake step at the drive that keeps the defender close enough to recover. Lecture 4.4.





Action 3: The 45 cut: when the defender looks at the drive, cut behind him.



The back cut is the cut made against denial. A defender who is determined to stop a player catching the ball plays high, between his man and the passer, with an arm in the passing lane. That is the one moment he cannot see the rim, and the man he is guarding cuts behind him to it, as in Figure 4. It is also called the back door. Every read-based offense has a rule that says a denied player back cuts, because a defender who denies has already given up the rim.






Figure 4: The back cut. The wing’s defender plays high to deny the catch. The wing cuts back door behind him to the rim for a bounce pass.









Setup


A player one pass from the ball whose defender is denying the pass, high and in the lane.


Trigger


The defender’s hand is in the passing lane and his weight is toward the ball.


Read


The cutter takes one step toward the ball to bring the defender higher, then plants and cuts to the rim. The passer reads: cutter open, the bounce pass; the rim protector steps up, the cutter’s spot has emptied and the cutter’s teammate fills it; the defender recovers, the cutter continues through to the far side and the floor is reset.


Payoff


A layup against a defender who chose to deny the pass rather than protect the rim.


Beaten by


Denying with the ball-side foot and hand only, staying half a step lower than the man so the back cut is contested; or top-locking only when help is under the rim. Lecture 4.4.





Action 4: The back cut: the defender who denies has turned his back on the rim.



The flash is the cut into the empty spot. When the defense sags toward the ball, or shifts as a zone does, a spot opens up, usually at the free-throw line or the elbow, and a player on the weak side cuts across the lane into it and catches facing the basket, as in Figure 5. Against a zone the flash is the whole offense, which is why it is in lecture 3.12 as well; against man-to-man it is how a big gets the ball at the elbow to run the high-low of Section 4.






Figure 5: The flash. The defense has sagged toward the ball and left the free-throw line empty. The weak-side big flashes across the lane into it and catches facing the basket.









Setup


The ball on one side. A weak-side player, usually a big, on the block or the wing. An empty spot near the free-throw line, because the defense has shifted toward the ball.


Trigger


The spot opens: a defender leaves it to help, or a zone shifts.


Read


The flasher cuts into the spot with hands up. The passer reads: flasher open, the pass; the flasher’s defender beats him to the spot, the flasher turns and seals for a lob or cuts through to the other side. On the catch the flasher reads the low post behind the defense for the high-low, then the shot, then the drive.


Payoff


The ball in the middle of the defense, facing the basket, with the defense on the move.


Beaten by


A defender who bumps the flasher as he crosses the lane and keeps a body between him and the ball; in a zone, the middle defender whose job is exactly that spot. Lecture 4.6.





Action 5: The flash: cut into the spot the defense left.



The stampede cut is a cut made to the ball rather than away from it. A player about to receive a pass has a defender closing out at him from the paint. Instead of catching and then deciding, he is already moving toward the rim as the pass arrives, so he catches at full speed and goes straight past a defender who is still decelerating, as in Figure 6. It exists because closeouts got long: a defender who has helped in the paint has fifteen feet to cover to get back to his man, and a man who is moving when he catches makes those fifteen feet impossible.






Figure 6: The stampede cut. The wing’s defender is closing out from the paint. The wing is already sprinting to the rim as the pass arrives and catches at full speed past a defender who cannot change direction.









Setup


A player on the perimeter whose defender has sunk into the paint to help. The ball with a passer who can see him.


Trigger


The passer picks him up and the defender starts to close out.


Read


The receiver starts his drive before the catch, toward the rim, at an angle past the closing defender. He catches on the move. If the defender is closing out square, the receiver goes by him. If the defender has stopped short and stayed low, the receiver pulls up. If the rim protector has stepped up, the receiver drops the ball off or kicks it out.


Payoff


A drive that beats the closeout before it happens.


Beaten by


A short, choppy closeout that never overruns the receiver, conceding the pull-up to stop the drive; or help so early the receiver is never left. Lecture 4.4.





Action 6: The stampede: catch already moving, and the closeout is beaten before it arrives.
crumbs: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
text:
3 Cuts that use a body
Two cuts use a teammate as an obstacle without a screen being set for them by name. In each, the teammate is standing where he was going to stand anyway, and the cutter runs past him so that his defender cannot.
The UCLA cut starts with a pass. The player at the top passes to the wing and then cuts down the lane line to the ball-side block, running his defender into the big standing at the elbow, as in Figure 7. The big’s stance is a back screen whether or not anyone called it one, and the cutter arrives on the block for a post feed from the wing. It is the entry to the high-post offense the cut is named for, and it appears in dozens of sets because it turns the point guard into a post threat with one pass.






Figure 7: The UCLA cut. The passer at the top feeds the wing and cuts down the lane line to the block, past the big at the elbow. The big’s body is a back screen on the cutter’s defender.









Setup


A guard at the top with the ball. A big at the ball-side elbow. A wing on that side to receive the pass.


Trigger


The pass to the wing; the guard’s defender turns to watch it.


Read


The guard cuts down the lane line past the big. If his defender is caught on the big, the guard posts on the block and the wing feeds him. If the defender goes under the big to the block first, the guard curls back to the elbow for a catch, or the big slips to the rim behind everyone. If the defense switches, the big’s defender has a guard on the block and the big has a mismatch at the elbow.


Payoff


A guard on the block with a defender behind him, or a big at the elbow with a small defender.


Beaten by


The defender jumping to the ball side of the big before the cut and riding the cutter to the block; or a switch. Lecture 4.5.





Action 7: The UCLA cut: pass to the wing, then down the lane line past the big.



The Iverson cut runs wing to wing across the top, over two bigs standing at the two elbows, as in Figure 8. The cutter’s defender has to get past two bodies in a row, and the cutter catches on the far wing already moving toward the basket side of the floor. It is named for the player it was designed to get the ball to, and the team that ran it did so because he was best with the ball moving into a catch rather than standing waiting for one. It is also called a Piston cut.






Figure 8: The Iverson cut. The wing cuts across the top of the key over two bigs at the elbows to the far wing, and catches on the move. His defender has two bodies to get around.









Setup


Two bigs at the two elbows. The ball at the top or the far slot. The cutter on one wing.


Trigger


The cutter runs at the near elbow.


Read


The cutter goes over both bigs. If his defender trails, he catches on the far wing and attacks the closeout. If the defender goes under the bigs to beat him to the far wing, the cutter stops at the second big and curls it to the rim. If a big’s defender switches onto the cutter, that big slips to the rim.


Payoff


A catch on the far wing at speed, with the defender two bodies behind, and the whole side of the floor ahead of the cutter.


Beaten by


The defender going under both bigs along the free-throw line and meeting the cutter at the far wing, conceding the curl; or switching at the second elbow. Lecture 4.5.





Action 8: The Iverson cut: wing to wing, over both elbows, catching on the move.
crumbs: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
text:
4 Two-man passing actions
Give and go is the oldest two-man action in the sport: pass, cut to the rim, get it back, as in Figure 9. It works because a defender relaxes for one step when his man gives up the ball, and one step is enough. The get action of lecture 3.2 is the give and go with a handoff in place of the return pass.






Figure 9: Give and go. The player at the top passes to the wing; his defender relaxes and turns to the ball. The passer cuts to the rim and takes the return pass.









Setup


Two players one pass apart, with the lane empty behind the passer’s defender.


Trigger


The pass; the passer’s defender takes his one step off.


Read


The passer cuts to the rim. If his defender is late, the return pass. If his defender recovers to the cut, the passer continues through and the floor resets with the ball on the wing. If the rim protector steps up to the cutter, the receiver drives the space he left.


Payoff


A layup two passes after the possession began.


Beaten by


Jumping to the ball on the pass, so the defender is between his man and the rim before the cut starts, which is the first rule of every man-to-man defense. Lecture 4.4.





Action 9: Give and go: pass, cut, get it back.



High-low is the two-big passing action. One big is at the high post, the free-throw line or an elbow; the other is at the low post on a block. The ball goes to the high post, and as it arrives the low post seals his defender on his hip, so that the high post can drop the ball over the top to him at the rim, as in Figure 10. Against a defense that fronts the low post, the high-low is the answer: the fronting defender is in front, the seal holds him there, and the pass comes from above where he cannot reach it.






Figure 10: High-low. The wing feeds the high post at the free-throw line. The low post seals his defender on his hip as the pass arrives, and the high post drops the ball over the top to him.









Setup


One big at the high post, one at the low post on the opposite block. The ball on a wing with a passing angle to the high post.


Trigger


The pass to the high post.


Read


The low post seals his defender as the ball is in the air, holding him on the hip away from where the pass will come. The high post catches and reads: the seal held, the pass over the top; the defender fought around to the high side, the low post steps to the baseline side for a bounce pass; the help came from the weak side, the shooter it left is open for a skip. If nothing is there, the high post faces up and the action is a pinch post.


Payoff


A catch at the rim against a defender who has been sealed, thrown from an angle the seal made safe.


Beaten by


The low defender playing behind rather than fronting, so there is no seal to hold; or the weak-side low man arriving on the catch. Lecture 4.4.





Action 10: High-low: the high post catches, the low post seals, the pass goes over the top.

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
section: 5 Movements that keep the floor spaced
text:
5 Movements that keep the floor spaced
Two entries in this lecture are not cuts to score. They are movements a player makes so that the cuts and drives around him work.
The lift is the corner player’s move when the ball is driven baseline on his side. If he stays in the corner, the driver has no pass: the defender who helps on the drive comes from the corner, and the corner is then covered by the rim protector’s rotation. If he lifts to the wing as the drive starts, he is a kick-out target the help defender has to leave to guard, and the drive gets a second option. The lift is a spacing rule, not a cut: the player is moving to stay one pass away from the ball.
The pinch post is the big catching at the weak-side elbow, facing the ball, with nobody else on his side of the floor. From there he has a handoff for a guard cutting past him, a shot, a drive, or the pass to a back cutter, and the offenses that use it, the Princeton and the triangle of lecture 3.9, use it as the hub of everything on that side. It is a spot as much as an action, and it is named here so that the phrase means something when it is heard.

title: 3.7: Cuts, Seals, Handoffs and Post Play
section: 6 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
text:
6 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
The glossaries describe several more cuts and post actions by one publisher only, so each has a description here and no entry until a second source names it. The diff is data/sources/glossary_diff_2026-09-21.md.

Curl, fade, straight, and the V-cut and L-cut. The first three are the reads off a screen taught in lecture 3.5. A V-cut is a perimeter player stepping in toward the rim and exploding back out to receive; an L-cut runs up the lane line and out to the wing. They are how a player without a screen gets open for a perimeter catch.
Shallow cut. A cut made in front of the ball to a new spot beside the handler, so the two exchange positions; the wave is its cousin, a cut made to create a double gap.
Rub and brush screen. A cut made so the cutter or his defender gets in the path of a different defender without contact, so it works like a screen but is not one under the rules.
Duck-in. A post player stepping into the lane and sealing his defender with his inside foot the moment the defender is in a help position.
Slice. A cut from the opposite corner through the lane, sometimes off a screen, to the top of the key.
Split cut. After a post entry, the two perimeter players nearest the post screen for one another and cut in opposite directions, so the post has two cutters to read.
Barkley. Dribbling from the perimeter into the block for a post-up, as the player it is named for did.
Boomerang. A pass to a teammate followed by an immediate return pass, so the original handler has a live dribble again, usually to attack a mismatch after a switch.
Dive, reverse seal, basket cut. A dive is a cut from the high post to the low post; a reverse seal is the low post holding his defender on the outside hip as the ball is reversed, which is the seal the high-low depends on; a basket cut is any hard cut to the rim.

The idea to carry into lecture 3.8 is that the screens of lectures 3.5 and 3.6 and the cuts of this one are what a team’s set plays are made of. The next lecture is about the sets themselves: the alignments a team starts from and the scripts it runs from them.

title: 3.13: Late Clock, Offense
text:
New terms introduced (2): 2-for-1, Late clock. Diagrams: 1.
This chapter has treated the defense as the thing an offense is working against. In the last seconds of a shot clock or a quarter, it is not. The constraint is the clock, and the clock changes which shot is a good shot. A contested mid-range jumper with two seconds left is not a bad decision; it is the best remaining option, and judging it against the shot an offense could have had with eighteen seconds left is a category error.
This lecture is short by design. It has two entries and no diagrams of actions, because nothing new happens on the floor: the actions are the ones already taught, run faster and with fewer options. What changes is the arithmetic.

title: 3.13: Late Clock, Offense
text:
1 The late-clock possession
Late clock is the state, not an action: the shot clock is under about seven seconds and the offense has to produce a shot rather than an advantage. Three things follow.
The order of preference inverts. For most of a possession an offense passes up a contested two to find an open three or a layup. Late, a contested two taken with two seconds left is worth more than a better shot that does not get taken, because a shot-clock violation is worth nothing at all.
The actions shrink. There is no time for the motion offense of lecture 3.11 to produce anything, so teams run a ball screen or an isolation: one action, one read, a shot. The snake and the step-up screen of lecture 3.3 are common here because each produces a shot from one dribble.
The offensive rebound is worth more. A missed shot with one second on the shot clock and fifteen on the game clock is a live ball with a fresh fourteen if it is tipped out, which is why teams send more players to the glass late than they would otherwise. That is the other half of the crash or get back decision of lecture 4.1.






Setup


Under about seven seconds on the shot clock, the ball in the hands of the player the team wants shooting, the floor spaced so one action can be run without a second pass.


Trigger


The clock, not the defense.


Read


One action and one read. If the first read is covered, the second is a shot rather than another action. The passer’s rule inverts too: a pass that takes two seconds off the clock to create a marginally better shot is a bad pass late and a good one early.


Payoff


A shot, taken, with a player on the glass.


Beaten by


A defense that switches everything and concedes nothing quickly, which is exactly what defenses do late; and by a defense that simply runs the clock out by not fouling and not gambling. Lecture 4.9.





Action 1: Late clock: one action, one read, and take the shot.

title: 3.13: Late Clock, Offense
text:
2 The 2-for-1
The 2-for-1 is arithmetic rather than tactics, as in Figure 1. Near the end of a quarter, if the offense shoots early enough, it will get the ball back for a second possession before the period ends; if it does not, the opponent gets the last shot and the offense gets one. The rule of thumb is that with about thirty-five seconds left, a shot taken by about twenty-eight seconds leaves time for the opponent’s possession and a final one of your own.






Figure 1: The 2-for-1. With about thirty seconds left in the quarter, the shot goes up early, one player crashes the glass and the rest get back, so the possession that follows still leaves time for one more.









Setup


The end of a quarter, roughly thirty to thirty-eight seconds on the game clock, the offense with the ball.


Trigger


The game clock, read by the point guard as the possession starts.


Read


Shoot by about twenty-eight seconds. The shot itself is chosen the way any late-clock shot is: quickly, from one action. The rest of the team splits, one or two to the offensive glass and the others to floor balance, because the second possession only exists if the opponent’s is not a layup.


Payoff


Two possessions to the opponent’s one, which is worth roughly one point of expected value at average efficiency, and more if the extra shot is a good one.


Beaten by


A defense that holds the ball itself on the possession in between, shooting with two or three seconds left, so the offense’s extra possession is a heave; and by a rushed shot so bad that the 2-for-1 costs more than it gains, which is the common failure.





Action 2: The 2-for-1: shoot early so the period ends with your possession, not theirs.



That is the end of the offense. Chapter 4 takes the same possession from the other side, in the same order: transition defense first, then defending early offense, then the coverages built for the ball screens of lectures 3.3 and 3.4, the help and rotations that answer the drives and cuts of lectures 3.7 and 3.10, the switching schemes that answer the screens of lectures 3.5 and 3.6, zones, presses, and the defensive halves of the special situations and the late clock. Every “beaten by” slot in this chapter names the lecture in Chapter 4 where its coverage is taught.

title: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
text:
New terms introduced (5): Elevator screen, Floppy, Hammer, Loop, Wedge. Diagrams: 5.
Lecture 3.5 was a parts list. This lecture is what teams build from it. A named off-ball action is two or three of those screens run in a sequence, for a particular player, with a particular pass at the end, and the name is shorthand a team uses so that five players can start it with one word. The names below are the ones heard most often on a broadcast, and each is taken apart here into the screens it is made of, so that a reader who has the parts can recognize any combination, named or not.
Section 1 is the elevator, two screens that close. Section 2 is the hammer, a back screen on the weak side of a drive. Section 3 is floppy, a shooter’s choice of sides. Section 4 is the loop, a stagger run along the baseline. Section 5 is the wedge, an off-ball screen that becomes a ball screen. Section 6 names the actions heard for which this site has a description but not yet an entry.

title: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
text:
1 Elevator: two screens that close
The elevator screen is two screeners standing side by side with a gap between them. The shooter runs through the gap, and the moment he is through the two screeners step together and close it, so the defender chasing him runs into two bodies with no way round, as in Figure 1 and Figure 2. It is also called elevator doors. It is the only screen in the sport that is set after the cutter has passed it, and it is legal only if both screeners are stationary when the defender arrives, which is why the timing of the step is everything.






Figure 1: Elevator, first frame. Two bigs stand at the free-throw line with a gap between them. The shooter runs up from the block through the gap; his defender is behind him.









Figure 2: Elevator, second frame. The two bigs step together the moment the shooter is through. His defender meets two screeners shoulder to shoulder, and the shooter catches at the top for a shot.









Setup


Two screeners at the free-throw line or the elbows, a body’s width apart, facing the baseline. The shooter under the rim or on a block. The ball on a wing with a passer who can see the top of the key.


Trigger


The shooter runs at the gap. His defender, behind him, follows.


Read


The shooter goes through and the screeners close. If the defender is caught, the shooter catches and shoots at the top. If the defender anticipates and goes round the outside of one screener, the shooter curls the other way, toward the side the defender did not choose. If the defense switches, one screener’s defender jumps out to the shooter and that screener slips to the rim behind him.


Payoff


A shooter at the top of the key with his defender stopped dead by two screens at once.


Beaten by


The defender refusing to follow through the gap and going round the outside before the doors close, conceding a step on the catch; or switching one screener’s defender onto the shooter as he comes through. Lecture 4.5.





Action 1: Elevator: two screens, one gap, closed behind the cutter.

title: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
section: 2 Hammer: the back screen on the weak side of a drive
text:
2 Hammer: the back screen on the weak side of a drive
The hammer joins a drive to a screen on the other side of the floor. The ball-handler drives baseline on one side. The weak-side shooter’s defender does what every help defender is taught to do and sinks toward the paint to stop the drive. As he sinks, a big back-screens him, and the shooter drifts down to the weak-side corner. The driver throws the pass along the baseline, under the rim, to the corner, as in Figure 3 and Figure 4. The hammer punishes the help rule itself: the defender who helped is screened for having helped.






Figure 3: Hammer, first frame. The ball-handler drives baseline on the right. On the left, the shooter’s defender sinks toward the paint to help, and the shooter starts to drift.









Figure 4: Hammer, second frame. The big back-screens the sinking defender; the shooter drifts to the left corner. The driver throws the baseline pass to the corner for an open three.









Setup


The ball on one wing with a driver. On the other side, a shooter on the wing and a big on the block or in the dunker spot. The strong-side corner empty or filled by a non-shooter who lifts.


Trigger


The driver turns the corner toward the baseline, and the weak-side wing defender takes his first step toward the paint.


Read


The big steps up behind the sinking defender and screens him; the shooter drifts to the corner. The driver reads as he reaches the baseline: shooter open in the corner, the baseline pass; defender fighting through the screen to the corner, the big is now alone under the rim for a drop-off; rim protector coming to the driver, the layup or the drop-off.


Payoff


A corner three on the weak side, thrown to a shooter whose defender was screened while helping.


Beaten by


The weak-side defender helping with his eyes and not his feet, staying home on the shooter and leaving the drive to the rim protector; or the X-out rotation in which the big’s defender takes the corner and the wing defender takes the big. Lecture 4.4.





Action 2: Hammer: the help defender is screened for helping, and the pass goes under the rim to the corner.
crumbs: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions

title: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
section: 3 Floppy: the shooter picks a side
text:
3 Floppy: the shooter picks a side
Floppy gives a shooter a choice. He starts under the rim. On one side of him is a single pin-down; on the other is a stagger. He reads his defender and runs off whichever side is open, as in Figure 5. The defender, who has to guard both sides at once, cannot be right about both, and the passer at the top waits for the read and delivers to whichever wing the shooter chose.






Figure 5: Floppy. The shooter starts under the rim. A single pin-down waits on one side and a stagger on the other. He reads his defender and runs one way; the pass from the top follows his choice.









Setup


The shooter under the rim, his defender behind him. A single screener on one block facing the baseline; two screeners in a line from the other block toward that wing. The ball at the top.


Trigger


The shooter’s first step. His defender shades one way to deny that side.


Read


The shooter goes the other way. Off the single screen, the four reads of lecture 3.5: curl, fade, straight, back cut. Off the stagger, the same reads at each screen, with the second screener able to slip if his defender jumps out. The passer at the top reads which side the shooter chose and which read he made, and throws to that spot.


Payoff


A shooter catching on the wing of his choosing with his defender behind at least one screen.


Beaten by


The defender going under everything and meeting the shooter at the wing, conceding the curl to take away the catch-and-shoot; or a defense that switches every screen so whichever side he picks, a fresh defender is waiting. Lecture 4.5.





Action 3: Floppy: one shooter, two sides, and a defender who has to guess.
crumbs: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions

title: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
section: 4 Loop: a stagger along the baseline
text:
4 Loop: a stagger along the baseline
The loop is a triple stagger run along the baseline. The cutter starts on one wing, runs down to the baseline, under the rim off three screens set along the lane, and up to the other wing for the catch, as in Figure 6. It is the longest cut in this chapter, and its length is the point: three screeners in a row along a path the defender has to run in full, with the ball waiting at the top for the catch at the far end.






Figure 6: Loop. Three screeners along the baseline side of the lane. The cutter runs from one wing down under the rim off all three and up to the other wing; his defender is three bodies behind.









Setup


The cutter on one wing. Three screeners along the baseline: one at each block and one under the rim, each facing the direction the cutter comes from. The ball at the top.


Trigger


The cutter runs to the baseline.


Read


The cutter runs off all three unless the defender does something that opens an earlier read: a defender going over the top of the first screen lets him curl into the lane; a defender going under lets him fade back to the wing he came from. Off the third screen he comes up to the far wing, and the passer delivers.


Payoff


A catch on the far wing with the defender trailing three screens.


Beaten by


The defender cutting across the lane under the screens to meet the cutter at the far wing, conceding the curl on the first screen; or a switch at any of the three. Lecture 4.5.





Action 4: Loop: three screens along the baseline, wing to wing.
crumbs: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions

title: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
section: 5 Wedge: the off-ball screen that becomes a ball screen
text:
5 Wedge: the off-ball screen that becomes a ball screen
The wedge is where the two kinds of screen meet. A guard sets an off-ball screen for the big, who cuts up to the top; as the big arrives he turns and sets a ball screen for the handler, as in Figure 7. The big’s defender has been screened once and is now late to a second screen, which is the same idea as the ram of lecture 3.4 with the first screen coming from a different direction: the ram pins the big down from above, the wedge screens him from the side.






Figure 7: Wedge. A guard screens the big’s defender; the big cuts up to the top and turns straight into a ball screen for the handler. His defender is late to the second screen.









Setup


The handler above the arc with the ball. The big on the block. A guard beside the big, ready to screen his defender.


Trigger


The guard’s screen lands on the big’s defender.


Read


The big cuts to the top and screens the ball. The handler comes off it. The reads are the pick-and-roll’s, with the big’s defender a step late: late to the level, the handler is downhill; sprinting to recover, the roller is behind him; switched at the first screen, a guard is guarding the ball screen and the big has a mismatch when he rolls.


Payoff


A pick-and-roll whose screener arrives with his defender screened.


Beaten by


Switching the first screen so the ball screen is guarded by whoever is nearest, or the big’s defender going under the first screen and beating the big to the top. Lecture 4.3 and lecture 4.5.





Action 5: Wedge: an off-ball screen for the big, then the big’s screen for the ball.

title: 3.6: Off-Ball Screens II: Named Off-Ball Actions
section: 6 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
text:
6 Names heard for which there is no entry yet
The following named off-ball actions are described by one publisher only. Under this site’s rule they have a description here and no card until a second independent source names them. The diff that decided this is data/sources/glossary_diff_2026-09-21.md.

Gaggle. A stagger in which the first screener, after screening, cuts to the opposite corner; the shooter runs through the screens and pops out for the shot. One glossary calls the screens split screens.
Baseline stagger. A single or double stagger set along the baseline for a shooter who fills the corner rather than coming up to the wing.
Picket fence. Three screeners in a line along the baseline, and a shooter who runs through all three, which is a loop with the screens set closer together.
Screen your own. Against a switching defense, a player screens his own defender so that defender cannot switch onto the cutter going by.
Fade. Turning down a screen and cutting away from it, which lecture 3.5 taught as one of the four reads rather than as an action of its own.

The idea to carry into lecture 3.7 is that not every off-ball movement is a screen. The next lecture is about cuts, seals and handoffs: what a player without the ball does to get open when nobody screens for him.

title: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions
text:
New terms introduced (5): Ghost screen, Ram, Slip, Spain pick-and-roll, Twist. Diagrams: 5.
Lecture 3.3 ended with the pick-and-roll as one action with one variable changed at a time. The actions in this lecture change the pick-and-roll itself. Each was built to beat a specific coverage from lecture 4.3 that had become good at guarding the plain version: the big who arrives at the level of the screen, the defender who drops to meet the roller, the two defenders who both jump to the screen the moment they see it coming. Each answer is a screen that arrives differently, a roller who is screened for, or a screen that is never set at all.
Section 1 is the ram, which screens the screener before the screen. Section 2 is the Spain pick-and-roll, which screens the roller’s defender after it. Section 3 is the pair that punish a defense for anticipating: the ghost screen and the slip. Section 4 is the twist, a second screen from the other side. Section 5 names the actions heard on broadcasts for which this site has a description but not yet an entry, so a reader knows what was said even where the database does not yet have a card.
crumbs: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions

title: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions
text:
1 Ram: screen the screener first
The coverage that arrives at the level of the screen depends on the big’s defender getting there. The ram stops him. Just before the big sets his ball screen, a wing sets a pin-down on the big’s defender, so the big sprints into the ball screen and his defender arrives a step late, as in Figure 1. The handler now comes off a screen that nobody is guarding at the level, and the drop coverage the defense wanted to play is a drop by a defender who is still running.






Figure 1: Ram. A wing pins down on the big’s defender; the big sprints off it straight into the ball screen. His defender arrives late, so the handler comes off with nobody at the level of the screen and the roll is open.









Setup


The handler at the top with the ball. The big on the block. A wing between the big and the top, ready to screen the big’s defender. The other two in the corners.


Trigger


The wing’s pin-down lands on the big’s defender as the big starts to sprint up.


Read


The big sets the ball screen while his defender is still behind the pin-down. The handler comes off it. If the big’s defender is late, the handler is at the free-throw line with nobody in front of him and the roller behind. If the big’s defender skips the pin-down and sprints to the ball, the pin-down screener is open where the big’s defender left him. If the defense switches the pin-down, the wing’s defender is now guarding the big’s ball screen, and a guard is guarding the big.


Payoff


A pick-and-roll in which the screener’s defender is a step late, which turns any coverage into a late one.


Beaten by


Switching the pin-down so the ball screen is guarded by whoever is nearest, which is the switching of lecture 4.5; or the big’s defender going under the pin-down and beating the big to the spot.





Action 1: Ram: a screen for the screener, so his defender arrives late to the screen that matters.
crumbs: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions

title: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions
text:
2 Spain: screen the roller’s defender
The drop coverage meets the roller with the big’s own defender dropping back. The Spain pick-and-roll takes that defender out. A third attacker, a shooter, starts under the ball screen at the free-throw line. As the big rolls, the shooter back-screens the dropping defender, so the roller is free to the rim; then the shooter pops out to the arc behind the play, so if the dropping defender’s teammate helps on the roller, the shooter is open at the top. It is also called the stack pick-and-roll, from the two players stacked at the top. Figure 2, Figure 3 and Figure 4 show the three beats.






Figure 2: Spain, first frame. A high pick-and-roll. A shooter stands at the free-throw line under the screen, which the defense reads as one more player to guard.









Figure 3: Spain, second frame. As the big rolls, the shooter back-screens the dropping defender. The roller is now free to the rim.









Figure 4: Spain, third frame. The shooter pops to the arc after his screen. The handler has the roller at the rim or the shooter at the top, and both defenders are a step late.









Setup


A high pick-and-roll at the top, with a shooter at the free-throw line below the screen and the other two attackers in the corners.


Trigger


The big rolls and his defender drops to meet him.


Read


The shooter back-screens the dropping defender and pops. The handler reads two things. If the back screen lands, the roller is open at the rim: throw the lob. If the dropping defender fights over the back screen to stay with the roller, or a corner defender comes to the rim, the shooter is open at the arc. If the shooter’s own defender stays with the shooter and never helps, the action is a plain pick-and-roll against a drop with one fewer help defender.


Payoff


A roller whose defender has been screened, and a shooter at the arc guarded by a defender who just got screened for.


Beaten by


Switching the back screen, so the shooter’s defender takes the roller and the dropping big takes the shooter; or the ball defender going under the first screen so the handler never turns the corner and the back screen has nobody to screen. Lecture 4.3 and lecture 4.5.





Action 2: Spain: the drop coverage’s own defender is screened, and the screener then becomes a shooter.
crumbs: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions

title: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions
section: 3 Ghost and slip: punishing the defense for arriving early
text:
3 Ghost and slip: punishing the defense for arriving early
Both of these actions start with a screener who never screens. They exist because good coverages start before the screen is set: the handler’s defender steps up to fight over it, the big’s defender steps up to meet the ball. Two defenders who have moved toward a screen that has not yet happened are two defenders who can be left behind.
The ghost screen leaves them behind toward the arc. The screener runs at the handler’s defender as if to screen, makes no contact, and keeps going, out to the three-point line on the other side of the ball, as in Figure 5. The handler’s defender has gone over a screen that never came and is behind the ball. The screener’s defender has dropped to help on a roll that never comes. The ghost is open at the arc for a pass and a three, or the handler drives into the space both defenders vacated.






Figure 5: The ghost screen. The screener sprints at the handler’s defender as if to screen, makes no contact, and runs out to the arc. Both defenders have moved to guard a screen that never happened.









Setup


The handler above the arc with the ball. A screener who can shoot arriving as if to set a ball screen. The other three spaced away.


Trigger


The handler’s defender adjusts his feet to fight over the coming screen, or the big’s defender steps up to hedge it.


Read


The screener veers past without contact and runs to the arc. The handler drives into the gap the two defenders left. If the big’s defender recovers to the ghost, the drive is open. If he stays home, the pass out to the ghost is an open three. If the handler’s defender switches onto the ghost, the handler has a big guarding him on the drive.


Payoff


Two defenders committed to a screen that did not happen, and a shooter or a driver in the space they left.


Beaten by


Defenders who guard the screen only once it is set, which costs them against a real screen, or a switch called early enough that the ghost is picked up as he arrives. Lecture 4.3.





Action 3: The ghost screen: a screen that is only threatened, and two defenders who guarded the threat.



The slip leaves them behind toward the rim. It is the same fake, aimed the other way: the screener approaches, both defenders jump up to the screen, and the screener cuts straight to the rim behind both of them, as in Figure 6. The pass is over the top, and the finish is a layup or a lob. A team that slips well makes the defense hesitate on every screen, which is what the plain pick-and-roll of lecture 3.3 needs to work.






Figure 6: The slip. Both defenders have jumped up to guard the coming screen. The screener never sets it and cuts to the rim behind them; the pass goes over the top.









Setup


A screener approaching the handler’s defender, with the paint empty.


Trigger


The screener sees both defenders step up to the screen before it is set: the handler’s defender to fight over it, his own defender to hedge or trap.


Read


The screener cuts to the rim. The handler passes over the top if the lane is empty; if the low man has rotated to the rim, the corner the low man left is open for a skip pass.


Payoff


A layup or a lob against two defenders who are above the play.


Beaten by


The big’s defender staying between the screener and the rim until the screen is actually set, which is the discipline behind the drop; or a low man who tags the slip early. Lecture 4.3 and lecture 4.4.





Action 4: The slip: the screen is never set, and the screener is at the rim before the defense knows it.

title: 3.4: On-Ball Screens II: Named Ball-Screen Actions
section: 4 Twist: the second screen from the other side
text:
4 Twist: the second screen from the other side
The twist gives the defense the same problem twice, in opposite directions. The handler comes off a ball screen going one way; his defender fights over and the big’s defender drops or hedges toward that side. The screener immediately turns and sets a second screen on the other side of the handler, and the handler crosses back the other way off it, as in Figure 7. Both defenders have committed to the first direction and now have to recover against the second. It is also called a re-screen, and a flip when the screener changes the angle of the same screen without resetting.






Figure 7: Twist. The handler comes off the first screen going left; both defenders commit that way. The screener turns and re-screens on the other side, and the handler crosses back right against two defenders who are leaning the wrong way.









Setup


A high pick-and-roll with the floor spaced, and a screener quick enough to reset.


Trigger


The handler comes off the first screen and both defenders lean toward that side.


Read


The screener turns and sets the second screen on the handler’s other shoulder. The handler crosses back off it. If the ball defender is now trailing, the handler is downhill against the big alone. If the big’s defender has stepped up to stop the crossover, the screener rolls behind him. If the defense had iced the first screen toward the sideline, the second screen sends the handler back toward the middle, which is where ice did not want him.


Payoff


A second pick-and-roll against two defenders who have already spent their first step on the first one.


Beaten by


The ball defender going under the second screen and conceding the pull-up, or a big who plays both screens at the level and never leans. Lecture 4.3.





Action 5: Twist: the same screen twice, in opposite directions, before the defense has recovered from the first.
